x.sub: Toxicology → Cardiac toxicity → Drug-induced long QT
x.intro: Many common ICU drugs block the cardiac potassium channel (hERG) that ends the action potential. Repolarisation is delayed, the QT lengthens, and an early afterdepolarisation can set off torsades de pointes. The risk is cumulative: each extra drug — quinolone, macrolide, azole, antipsychotic, tricyclic — a low potassium or magnesium, or a raised drug level adds to it.
why: **Citalopram and escitalopram.** Among the SSRIs these two prolong the QT in a dose-dependent way, so torsades on an SSRI means citalopram. Sertraline is the usual choice when cardiac risk is a concern.

**Thioridazine and ziprasidone; IV haloperidol is dangerous at high doses.** Thioridazine (a typical) and ziprasidone (an atypical) prolong QTc the most, so the class is not what matters: the pooled arrhythmia risk of typical and atypical antipsychotics is similar, while QTc prolongation varies drug by drug. Oral haloperidol carries modest risk, but large intravenous doses have caused torsades.

**The one that also blocks CYP3A4 (erythromycin, fluconazole) — it raises the others’ levels.** Such a drug prolongs the QT itself and slows the clearance of other QT drugs, so removing it removes two sources of risk at once. When no drug on the list inhibits CYP3A4, stop the strongest hERG blocker: a tricyclic before aripiprazole (minimal QT effect), carvedilol (none) or omeprazole (only through low magnesium).

**Potassium and magnesium.** Low potassium enhances hERG block and low magnesium makes afterdepolarisations more likely. Correcting both raises the threshold for torsades, and intravenous magnesium is the first treatment once torsades occurs.
mimic: Long QT vs wide QRS
A long QT is potassium-channel block (stop the drug, give magnesium); a wide QRS is sodium-channel block (bicarbonate). Osborn waves mean hypothermia, a long PR the AV node.
traps: “Typical antipsychotics carry more arrhythmia risk than atypicals”
The risk is similar; thioridazine and ziprasidone, one from each class, prolong QTc most (only 3% chose this on DocT GT).
“With a long QT, stop the antipsychotic first”
Aripiprazole barely affects the QT; stop the strongest hERG blocker — here amitriptyline (67% on DocT GT).
“Correcting potassium is enough”
Magnesium must be corrected too.
decode: Pneumonia on ciprofloxacin; carvedilol, omeprazole, aripiprazole, amitriptyline; long QT — stop first? [DocT GT]
Amitriptyline.
ICU patient on moxifloxacin, fluconazole, then erythromycin — likely ECG finding? [DocT GT]
Widened QT.
Arrhythmia risk: typical vs atypical antipsychotics [DocT GT]
No difference.
Torsades on an SSRI: which? [Marrow]
Citalopram.
x.punch: QT risk adds up, so remove the drug that multiplies the others — or the strongest hERG blocker — first, then correct potassium and magnesium.

topups.q:
**Carbon monoxide vs methaemoglobin:**
**a** SpO₂ in CO
**b** SpO₂ in MetHb, and why
**c** Common drug causes of MetHb
**d** Treatment of MetHb, and its contraindication
**e** Hyperbaric oxygen in CO: when?
a: **a** **Falsely normal** — COHb looks like oxyhaemoglobin; PaO₂ normal.
**b** **Drifts toward ~85%** as MetHb rises — it absorbs equally at 660 and 940 nm.
**c** **Benzocaine/prilocaine** before endoscopy, dapsone, nitrites/nitrates, primaquine, rasburicase.
**d** **Methylene blue 1–2 mg/kg** if symptomatic or MetHb >20–30%; **never in G6PD deficiency**.
**e** COHb **>25%** (>15% in pregnancy), loss of consciousness, ischaemia or neurological signs.

x.sub: Toxicology → Gases and haemoglobin → Carbon monoxide vs methaemoglobin
x.intro: A pulse oximeter estimates saturation from the ratio of light absorbed at two wavelengths, 660 and 940 nm, and assumes only oxyhaemoglobin and deoxyhaemoglobin are present. Carbon monoxide and methaemoglobin both add a third haemoglobin that carries no oxygen. The oximeter misreads them in opposite directions, and that difference is what the exam tests.
why: **Falsely normal — COHb looks like oxyhaemoglobin; PaO₂ normal.** Carboxyhaemoglobin absorbs red light much as oxyhaemoglobin does, so it is counted as saturated; PaO₂ measures dissolved oxygen, which is normal. Only co-oximetry (or, classically, the Hoppe-Seyler alkali test) shows COHb.

**Drifts toward ~85% as MetHb rises — it absorbs equally at 660 and 940 nm.** An equal absorption ratio corresponds to a reading of about 85%, so SpO₂ settles there however high the MetHb climbs, with a normal PaO₂ and chocolate-brown blood.

**Benzocaine/prilocaine before endoscopy, dapsone, nitrites/nitrates, primaquine, rasburicase.** These oxidise haem iron from ferrous to ferric, which cannot bind oxygen. Topical anaesthetic sprays are the classic cause; paracetamol, atropine and digoxin are not causes.

**Methylene blue 1–2 mg/kg if symptomatic or MetHb >20–30%; never in G6PD deficiency.** Methylene blue is reduced to leucomethylene blue by an NADPH-dependent reductase, and this reduces methaemoglobin. The NADPH comes from G6PD; without it the drug fails and can haemolyse — ascorbic acid is the alternative. It is also an MAO inhibitor, so it can precipitate serotonin syndrome in a patient on an SSRI.

**COHb >25% (>15% in pregnancy), loss of consciousness, ischaemia or neurological signs.** Hyperbaric oxygen shortens the COHb half-life and is given to reduce delayed neurological sequelae; without these features, normobaric 100% oxygen for about 6 hours is enough. The only absolute contraindication is an untreated pneumothorax; COPD and prior bleomycin are relative.
mimic: CO vs cyanide
Both give a normal SpO₂ with tissue hypoxia; cyanide gives a very high lactate and high venous oxygen.
traps: “A normal SpO₂ excludes CO poisoning”
COHb reads as oxyhaemoglobin; send a co-oximetry sample.
“Methaemoglobinaemia gives a low PaO₂”
PaO₂ is normal; the SpO₂ sits near 85%.
“Methylene blue works in everyone”
It needs NADPH from G6PD; in deficiency it fails and haemolyses — use ascorbic acid (43% on DocT).
“COHb 12% — hyperbaric oxygen”
Without high-risk features, 100% oxygen by mask for about 6 hours.
decode: A patient with methaemoglobinaemia will show [DocT GT]
Pulse oximetry around 85%.
Which drug causes methaemoglobinaemia: paracetamol, benzocaine, atropine, digoxin? [DocT GT]
Benzocaine.
Chemical-factory worker with cyanosis — true statement [DocT]
Ascorbic acid is used in G6PD deficiency.
Painter, CO exposure, COHb 12%, no high-risk features [Marrow]
High-flow oxygen for 6 hours.
x.punch: The oximeter cannot see what it was not built for: carbon monoxide reads as normal, methaemoglobin as about 85%, and only co-oximetry tells the truth.

topups.q:
**Toxic alcohol: block or dialyse?**
**a** When to give fomepizole
**b** Does a normal osmolal gap exclude it?
**c** Why ethanol lets fomepizole wait
**d** When to dialyse
a: **a** **Empirically** when a toxic alcohol is suspected and the level is delayed.
**b** **No** — in a late presenter the alcohol is already metabolised to acid.
**c** Ethanol **≥100 mg/dL** saturates alcohol dehydrogenase (10–20× higher affinity).
**d** **Visual signs, AKI or severe acidosis**.

x.sub: Toxicology → Toxic alcohols → Block or dialyse
x.intro: Methanol and ethylene glycol are not very toxic themselves. Alcohol dehydrogenase converts them to formic acid and glycolic and oxalic acids, which cause the acidosis, blindness and renal failure. Treatment therefore has two parts: stop the enzyme before acid forms, and remove the alcohol and acid once harm has started.
why: **Empirically when a toxic alcohol is suspected and the level is delayed.** Fomepizole blocks alcohol dehydrogenase, so no new acid forms while waiting; levels are rarely available quickly, and every hour of delay lets more acid form. A high anion gap acidosis with a large osmolal gap, no ethanol and no ketones means a fomepizole load now.

**No — in a late presenter the alcohol is already metabolised to acid.** As the alcohol is converted, the osmolal gap falls and the anion gap rises, and the normal range is wide, so a small toxic amount can hide inside it.

**Ethanol ≥100 mg/dL saturates alcohol dehydrogenase (10–20× higher affinity).** While ethanol is at this level the toxic alcohol is hardly metabolised, so fomepizole can be deferred and started as the ethanol falls.

**Visual signs, AKI or severe acidosis.** These show that acid has formed and is damaging organs. Haemodialysis removes both the parent alcohol and the acids, which fomepizole cannot do; fomepizole continues alongside (dosed more often during dialysis). A pH of 7.10 with a raised creatinine means dialysis even if the level is under 50 mg/dL.
mimic: Toxic alcohol vs alcoholic ketoacidosis
Both give high anion gap acidosis in a drinker; ketoacidosis has ketones and a small osmolal gap.
Isopropanol
Raises the osmolal gap but makes acetone, a ketone, not an acid — no acidosis, so a patient who stays comatose with a normal pH has isopropanol, and needs no fomepizole.
traps: “Wait for the level before fomepizole”
Give it on suspicion; delay lets acid form.
“Moonshine with ethanol 453 mg/dL — fomepizole now”
Ethanol already blocks the enzyme; fomepizole can be deferred (37% on DocT GT).
“Severe anion gap acidosis — dialysis is the immediate therapy”
A fomepizole load starts immediately (33% on DocT GT); dialysis is added for the acidosis or organ damage.
“Fomepizole is enough once acidosis or blindness is established”
Established acid and organ damage need dialysis.
decode: Windshield-fluid ingestion, asymptomatic, methanol level 24 h away [Marrow]
Give fomepizole.
Confused, severe anion gap acidosis, osmolal gap 32, ethanol zero, no ketones — start immediately? [DocT GT]
Fomepizole loading dose.
Oxycodone, liquor and moonshine, ethanol 453 — why defer fomepizole? [DocT GT]
Ethanol.
Antifreeze, pH 7.10, creatinine 3.5, ethylene glycol 45 mg/dL [DocT GT]
Haemodialysis (with fomepizole).
x.punch: Block the enzyme early, while there is still alcohol to block; dialyse once the acid or the damage is already there.

topups.q: **Spot it:** hallucinations, BP 190/110, HR 129, sweating — urine drug screen **negative**.
a: **Synthetic cathinones** (bath salts, mephedrone) or **synthetic cannabinoids** — routine immunoassays miss them.
Benzodiazepines, cooling, fluids; watch hyperthermia, rhabdomyolysis, hyponatraemia.

x.sub: Toxicology → Toxidromes → Sympathomimetic with a negative screen
x.intro: A patient is agitated, hallucinating, hypertensive, tachycardic and sweating — a sympathomimetic toxidrome. The urine screen is negative for amphetamines and cocaine. That does not exclude a drug; it shows the limits of the test.
why: **Synthetic cathinones (bath salts, mephedrone) or synthetic cannabinoids — routine immunoassays miss them.** A urine immunoassay detects only the molecules its antibodies were made against. The standard panel picks up amphetamines (and usually MDMA), so a negative screen argues against them; cathinones are different enough to escape it. Severe hypertension and tachycardia make it a toxidrome, not a new psychosis.

**Benzodiazepines, cooling, fluids; watch hyperthermia, rhabdomyolysis, hyponatraemia.** Benzodiazepines reduce central sympathetic drive, lowering heart rate, blood pressure and heat production. Hyperthermia and rhabdomyolysis are the main causes of death; hyponatraemia, as with MDMA, can cause seizures.
mimic: Sympathomimetic vs anticholinergic
Both are hot, agitated and tachycardic; the sympathomimetic patient sweats, the anticholinergic patient has dry skin and urinary retention.
traps: “Negative screen, florid picture — ecstasy or amphetamine”
The standard screen detects those; synthetic cathinone is the answer (only 16% on DocT GT).
“Negative screen and hallucinations — new-onset schizophrenia”
BP 190/110 and HR 129 are a toxidrome.
“A β-blocker for the tachycardia”
Sedation with benzodiazepines comes first; it treats the cause.
decode: College student, floridly hallucinating, BP 190/110, HR 129, standard urine panel negative [DocT GT]
Synthetic cathinone intoxication.
Same stem — why not ecstasy, amphetamine or schizophrenia? [DocT GT]
The panel detects amphetamines and MDMA; the vital signs make it a toxidrome.
x.punch: A urine screen finds only what it was built to find; a sympathomimetic picture with a negative screen is still a sympathomimetic, and it is treated with sedation and cooling.

topups.q: **Spot it:** coma, pinpoint pupils, slow breathing, bradycardia — **no response to naloxone**.
a: **Clonidine** (central α₂ agonist).
Supportive care; atropine for bradycardia. Naloxone response is inconsistent.

x.intro: Coma, pinpoint pupils and slow breathing look like opioid poisoning, so naloxone is given. When it fails, the question becomes which drug produces the same picture through a different receptor.
why: **Clonidine (central α₂ agonist).** Clonidine stimulates brainstem α₂ receptors and reduces sympathetic outflow: miosis, sedation, respiratory depression, bradycardia and hypotension. Children are often poisoned by a single tablet or by imidazoline eye or nasal drops. Early transient hypertension can occur from peripheral α stimulation.

**Supportive care; atropine for bradycardia. Naloxone response is inconsistent.** Most patients recover within 24–48 hours with airway and circulatory support; atropine treats symptomatic bradycardia.
mimic: Clonidine vs benzodiazepine or organophosphate
Benzodiazepines do not give pinpoint pupils; organophosphates add wet secretions and fasciculation.
Clonidine vs pontine haemorrhage
Pontine haemorrhage also gives coma with pinpoint pupils; CT separates them.
traps: “Pinpoint pupils, no naloxone response — benzodiazepine”
Benzodiazepines do not cause pinpoint pupils; think clonidine.
“If naloxone fails, give more until it works”
Clonidine response is inconsistent; supportive care is the treatment.
decode: Comatose, pinpoint pupils, hypoventilation, no response to naloxone — next likely diagnosis? [DocT GT]
Clonidine toxicity.
Same stem — why not benzodiazepine, organophosphate or CO? [DocT GT]
No pinpoint pupils with benzodiazepines or CO; organophosphates are wet.
x.punch: Clonidine copies the opioid picture through a different receptor, so the opioid antidote is unreliable and care is supportive.

topups.q: **Spot it:** unconscious house-fire victim, lactate 12, SpO₂ 99%.
a: **Cyanide plus carbon monoxide**.
**Hydroxocobalamin 5 g** with 100% O₂ (intubate if GCS ≤8); **avoid nitrites** — their methaemoglobin worsens oxygen carriage.

x.sub: Toxicology → Smoke inhalation → Cyanide and carbon monoxide
x.intro: Burning wool, silk, plastics and foam release hydrogen cyanide as well as carbon monoxide. A house-fire victim can therefore have two poisons that both stop oxygen use, and neither lowers the pulse oximeter reading. The blood lactate is the clue.
why: **Cyanide plus carbon monoxide.** COHb reads as oxyhaemoglobin, so SpO₂ is normal. Cyanide blocks cytochrome oxidase, so cells cannot use oxygen; venous blood stays oxygenated and lactate rises. In smoke inhalation a lactate of about 8–10 mmol/L or more strongly suggests cyanide; convulsions and coma are common.

**Hydroxocobalamin 5 g with 100% O₂ (intubate if GCS ≤8); avoid nitrites — their methaemoglobin worsens oxygen carriage.** Hydroxocobalamin binds cyanide to form cyanocobalamin, excreted in urine; it is now first choice for any cyanide poisoning. Nitrites work by creating methaemoglobin, which, with CO already occupying haemoglobin, cuts oxygen delivery further; they are also vasodilators and worsen hypotension. Thiosulphate alone is safe.
mimic: Smoke victim vs simple CO poisoning
CO alone rarely gives a very high lactate; a lactate of 12 with shock points to cyanide.
traps: “Cyanide, lactate 12, hypotension — nitrite plus thiosulphate”
Hydroxocobalamin is first choice (42% on DocT).
“Smoke victim — the standard nitrite kit is fine”
Nitrite methaemoglobin adds to the CO deficit and lowers blood pressure; avoid it (55% on DocT GT).
“SpO₂ 99%, so oxygenation is fine”
COHb reads as oxyhaemoglobin and cyanide stops oxygen use, not delivery.
decode: Clothing-factory fire (wool, silk), ‘bitter almond’, convulsions — cyanide treatment to AVOID? [DocT GT]
Sodium nitrite.
Fire victim, cyanide with hypotension — avoid [Marrow]
3% sodium nitrite.
Industrial worker, unconscious, hypotensive, lactate 12, almond odour [DocT]
Hydroxocobalamin.
x.punch: In a fire victim with a normal SpO₂, the lactate gives cyanide away: give hydroxocobalamin and oxygen, never nitrites.

topups.q:
**Heavy metals in the ICU:**
**a** Arsenic: how it poisons
**b** Arsenic: the neuropathy and its mimic
**c** Arsenic: the test before treating ‘GBS’, and the chelator
**d** Lead encephalopathy: chelation order
**e** Mercury: swallowed vs inhaled
a: **a** Binds **sulfhydryl** groups (blocks pyruvate dehydrogenase); garlic odour, rice-water diarrhoea, QT prolongation.
**b** At 1–3 weeks an ascending **axonal** neuropathy that **mimics GBS**; Mees lines.
**c** **24-h urine arsenic** (blood clears in days); chelate with **dimercaprol**, then DMSA or DMPS.
**d** **Dimercaprol first, then CaNa₂EDTA 4 h later**; avoid LP and routine hyperventilation.
**e** Swallowed elemental (thermometer): **harmless**. Inhaled vapour: **pneumonitis, ARDS**, neurotoxicity.

x.sub: Toxicology → Heavy metals → Arsenic, lead, mercury
x.intro: Heavy metals poison enzymes by binding their sulfhydryl groups. In the ICU they appear as an unexplained gastroenteritis with arrhythmia, a neuropathy that looks like Guillain–Barré syndrome, or an encephalopathy. Chelators offer the metal a partner it binds more tightly, which is then excreted.
why: **Binds sulfhydryl groups (blocks pyruvate dehydrogenase); garlic odour, rice-water diarrhoea, QT prolongation.** Blocking pyruvate dehydrogenase stops aerobic energy production; capillary damage in the gut causes profuse watery diarrhoea, and the long QT leads to torsades.
**At 1–3 weeks an ascending axonal neuropathy that mimics GBS; Mees lines.** The neuropathy is sensorimotor and often painful; Mees lines are white transverse nail bands that appear weeks later.

**24-h urine arsenic (blood clears within hours to days); chelate with dimercaprol, then DMSA or DMPS.** Arsenic leaves the blood quickly, so a blood level at the neuropathy stage is often normal while urine still shows it.

**Dimercaprol first, then CaNa₂EDTA 4 h later; avoid LP and routine hyperventilation.** EDTA alone mobilises lead from tissues into the brain; dimercaprol first prevents this. Lead encephalopathy causes cerebral oedema, so lumbar puncture risks herniation.
**Swallowed elemental (thermometer): harmless. Inhaled vapour: pneumonitis, ARDS, neurotoxicity.** Elemental mercury is barely absorbed from the gut but is absorbed well through the lungs.
mimic: Arsenic neuropathy vs GBS
Both ascend; arsenic follows a gastrointestinal illness with QT prolongation and later Mees lines — check urine arsenic.
Arsenic vs thallium
Both give a painful neuropathy and Mees lines; thallium adds alopecia, including loss of the lateral eyebrows.
traps: “Normal blood arsenic excludes poisoning”
Blood clears in days; 24-hour urine is the test.
“EDTA alone for lead encephalopathy”
It can move lead into the brain; dimercaprol goes first.
decode: Hair loss, lateral eyebrow loss, behaviour change, nail lines [Marrow]
Thallium.
Vomiting and diarrhoea, then 2 weeks later ascending weakness [pattern]
Arsenic → 24-hour urine arsenic, dimercaprol.
x.punch: Metals poison by binding sulfhydryl groups and chelators offer them a better partner — but the route and the order of chelation decide whether that helps or harms.

topups.q:
**Iron poisoning:**
**a** Stage 1 (0–6 h)
**b** Stage 2 (6–24 h)
**c** Stage 3 (24–48 h)
**d** Late stages
**e** Decontamination and chelation
a: **a** **Corrosive GI**: vomiting, haematemesis, shock.
**b** **Latent** — apparent recovery while iron enters cells: the dangerous reassurance.
**c** **Shock, high anion gap acidosis**, hepatic necrosis, coagulopathy.
**d** Hepatic failure; **gastric outlet stricture** at 2–6 weeks.
**e** Not bound by charcoal (an ion) → **whole bowel irrigation**; tablets are radio-opaque; **deferoxamine** up to 15 mg/kg/h (vin-rosé urine), usually stopped by ~24 h (ARDS).

x.intro: Iron tablets are common in homes, and in children they are a classic cause of death from overdose. Iron first damages the gut directly, then enters the circulation and cells, where free iron damages mitochondria. The stages follow that path, and the quiet middle stage is where patients are wrongly sent home.
why: **Corrosive GI: vomiting, haematemesis, shock.** Iron is directly corrosive; fluid loss can cause early hypovolaemic shock. No gastrointestinal symptoms by 6 hours makes serious toxicity unlikely.
**Latent — apparent recovery while iron enters cells: the dangerous reassurance.** Gut symptoms settle, but a persistent acidosis or tachycardia shows that toxicity is progressing.

**Shock, high anion gap acidosis, hepatic necrosis, coagulopathy.** Free iron disrupts oxidative phosphorylation, so cells make lactate; the liver receives the iron first through the portal circulation.
**Hepatic failure; gastric outlet stricture at 2–6 weeks.** The early corrosive injury heals with scarring that can obstruct the pylorus.

**Not bound by charcoal (an ion) → whole bowel irrigation; tablets are radio-opaque; deferoxamine up to 15 mg/kg/h (vin-rosé urine), usually stopped by ~24 h (ARDS).** Deferoxamine chelates free iron into ferrioxamine, which the kidney excretes and which colours the urine. If AKI develops, haemodialysis removes the ferrioxamine complex — not the protein-bound iron — so chelation can continue.
mimic: Iron vs lithium
Neither is bound by charcoal and both get whole bowel irrigation; iron tablets are radio-opaque and give a corrosive gastroenteritis.
traps: “Symptoms have settled at 12 hours, so discharge”
That may be the latent stage; check acidosis and serum iron.
“Haemodialysis removes the iron”
It removes ferrioxamine; the iron itself is bound and in tissues.
“Continue deferoxamine until the urine clears”
Long infusions cause ARDS; usually stopped by about 24 hours.
decode: Severe iron poisoning on deferoxamine develops AKI — role of haemodialysis? [DocT GT]
Removes the ferrioxamine complex.
Iron reaction: mechanism of the drug needed [Marrow]
Chelation.
x.punch: Iron burns the gut, then hides in cells: a quiet middle stage is not recovery, so judge by the acidosis, not by how the patient looks.

topups.q:
**Caustic ingestion with hoarseness and drooling:**
**a** First step
**b** Then
**c** What not to do
**d** Steroids?
a: **a** **Secure the airway early** (fibreoptic or awake): laryngeal oedema worsens over hours.
**b** **Endoscopy within 12–24 h** for Zargar grading.
**c** No emesis, no charcoal, no neutralisation, no blind NG tube.
**d** No overall benefit; only a deep circumferential **grade IIb** burn may benefit — never grade III (masks perforation).

x.intro: A patient has swallowed a strong acid or alkali. The burn to the pharynx and larynx swells over the following hours, so a patient who is talking now can obstruct later. Hoarseness, stridor and drooling show that the larynx is already involved.
why: **Secure the airway early (fibreoptic or awake): laryngeal oedema worsens over hours.** Intubation gets harder as the oedema grows, and paralysing a patient with a distorted airway risks a can’t-intubate, can’t-oxygenate crisis, so spontaneous breathing is kept.
**Endoscopy within 12–24 h for Zargar grading.** Grading predicts stricture and perforation; the healing wall is weakest from roughly day 5 to day 15, when endoscopy is most dangerous.
**No emesis, no charcoal, no neutralisation, no blind NG tube.** Vomiting re-exposes the oesophagus, charcoal obscures endoscopy, neutralisation adds heat, and a blind tube can perforate.

**No overall benefit; only a deep circumferential grade IIb burn may benefit — never grade III (masks perforation).** Trials show no overall fall in strictures; in grade III necrosis steroids add infection risk and hide the signs of perforation.
traps: “No mouth burns, so no oesophageal injury”
The oesophagus can be burned without visible oral injury.
“Neutralise the alkali with a weak acid”
The reaction produces heat and worsens the burn.
decode: Drooling and hoarseness after drinking drain cleaner [pattern]
Secure the airway first.
Grade III on endoscopy — steroids? [pattern]
No.
x.punch: A caustic burn of the larynx swells while the patient still looks well, so the airway is secured first and the endoscopy grades everything else.

topups.q:
**SJS/TEN vs DRESS:**
**a** SJS vs TEN
**b** Timing after the drug
**c** The feature that marks DRESS
**d** Mucosa
**e** Treatment
a: **a** One spectrum by detachment: **SJS <10% · overlap 10–30% · TEN >30%** BSA.
**b** SJS/TEN **4–28 days**; DRESS **2–8 weeks**.
**c** **Eosinophilia** with fever, facial oedema, nodes and organ involvement (liver most).
**d** SJS/TEN: involved. DRESS: usually **spared**.
**e** SJS/TEN: stop the drug, burn-unit care (ciclosporin or IVIG may help). DRESS: stop the drug, **steroids with a slow taper**.

x.sub: Toxicology → Drug reactions → SJS/TEN vs DRESS
x.intro: Two severe drug reactions can bring a patient to the ICU with a rash and fever. SJS/TEN is widespread death of the epidermis and mucosa, behaving like a burn. DRESS is a delayed systemic hypersensitivity in which the internal organs carry the risk.
why: **One spectrum by detachment: SJS <10% · overlap 10–30% · TEN >30% BSA.** The name depends only on the area of skin that detaches, and mortality rises with it.
**SJS/TEN 4–28 days; DRESS 2–8 weeks.** DRESS appears later than almost any other drug rash, so the culprit is often a drug started a month or more before.
**Eosinophilia with fever, facial oedema, nodes and organ involvement (liver most).** DRESS is a systemic hypersensitivity, so blood and organs are affected; hepatitis is the commonest organ injury.
**SJS/TEN: involved. DRESS: usually spared.** Mucosal erosions of mouth, eyes and genitals are part of the epidermal necrosis of SJS/TEN.

**SJS/TEN: stop the drug, burn-unit care (ciclosporin or IVIG may help). DRESS: stop the drug, steroids with a slow taper.** The immune reaction drives DRESS organ damage and relapses, hence the slow taper.
traps: “The rash began 5 weeks after the drug, so it is not drug-induced”
DRESS typically appears at 2–8 weeks.
decode: Carbamazepine started 5 weeks ago; fever, facial oedema, eosinophilia, raised ALT [pattern]
DRESS → stop drug, steroids.
10 days after a new drug, oral erosions, 40% detachment [pattern]
TEN → burn unit.
x.punch: Timing and blood separate them: early skin and mucosal necrosis is SJS/TEN and is treated as a burn; late fever, eosinophils and organ injury is DRESS and is treated with a slow steroid taper.

topups.q:
**Quinine overdose:**
**a** First symptoms
**b** The classic exam feature
**c** ECG and treatment
**d** Glucose
**e** Elimination
a: **a** **Cinchonism**: tinnitus, deafness, nausea, headache.
**b** **Blindness** at 6–12 h, fixed dilated pupils.
**c** **Na⁺-channel block**: wide QRS, VT → **bicarbonate**.
**d** **Hypoglycaemia** (quinine releases insulin).
**e** **Multi-dose charcoal**; dialysis does not help.

x.intro: Quinine is still used for malaria and, in some places, for cramps. In overdose it behaves like other sodium-channel blockers on the heart, but it also damages the retina and stimulates insulin release.
why: **Cinchonism: tinnitus, deafness, nausea, headache.** The first sign of toxicity, even at high therapeutic levels.
**Blindness at 6–12 h, fixed dilated pupils.** Quinine is directly toxic to the retina.
**Na⁺-channel block: wide QRS, VT → bicarbonate.** Like tricyclics, quinine slows ventricular conduction; bicarbonate reduces drug binding to the channel.
**Hypoglycaemia (quinine releases insulin).** Low glucose can add to coma and seizures, so it is checked repeatedly.

**Multi-dose charcoal; dialysis does not help.** Repeated charcoal draws quinine back into the gut and shortens its half-life; quinine is widely distributed and protein-bound, so dialysis removes little. It is not a whole bowel irrigation drug.
mimic: Quinine vs tricyclic overdose
Both widen the QRS and respond to bicarbonate; quinine adds blindness, tinnitus and hypoglycaemia.
traps: “Whole bowel irrigation or dialysis for quinine”
Multi-dose charcoal is the elimination method.
decode: Whole bowel irrigation indications EXCEPT [Marrow]
Quinine overdose (multi-dose charcoal instead).
Overdose with tinnitus, then sudden blindness [pattern]
Quinine.
x.punch: Quinine is a sodium-channel blocker with two extras: it blinds and it releases insulin, so give bicarbonate for the QRS, glucose for the sugar, and charcoal, not dialysis.

topups.q:
**Lamotrigine or carbamazepine overdose:**
**a** Why they can CAUSE seizures
**b** ECG

why: **At toxic levels the Na⁺ block silences inhibitory interneurons → paradoxical seizures.** The proposed explanation: fast-firing inhibitory interneurons depend most on sodium channels and are suppressed first, releasing excitatory neurons.
**Wide QRS — the same block in the heart.** Cardiac sodium channels conduct the impulse through the ventricles, so blocking them widens the QRS and risks VT.
**Benzodiazepines, then phenobarbital or propofol.** These act on GABA-A receptors; phenytoin is avoided because it is itself a sodium-channel blocker.
**Bicarbonate; lipid if refractory.** Raising extracellular sodium and pH reduces drug binding and narrows the QRS.

x.intro: After whole-body radiation, cells that divide rapidly die first, because radiation damages DNA and the damage shows when a cell tries to divide. APAP-01.intro: Paracetamol is safe at therapeutic doses because the liver has more than enough capacity to make it harmless. Toxicity is a matter of dose per kilogram: once the ingested amount outruns that capacity, a toxic metabolite accumulates. The thresholds mark where risk begins, where it becomes near-certain, and how severe injury is defined.
why: **Maximum therapeutic dose 4 g/day in adults; 75 mg/kg/day in children.** At these doses conjugation handles almost all of the drug, and the small oxidised fraction is mopped up by glutathione without depleting it.

**Toxic single dose: >150 mg/kg, or 7.5–10 g in an adult.** Above this the conjugation pathways saturate, more of the dose is oxidised, and NAPQI uses up glutathione faster than the liver can make it (APAP-02).

**Liver failure almost certain above 350 mg/kg (untreated).** Glutathione is exhausted early and NAPQI binds hepatocyte proteins in large amounts; without N-acetylcysteine severe hepatotoxicity is the rule.
**Severe hepatotoxicity: peak AST or ALT >1000 U/L.** A peak above 1000 marks substantial necrosis; it is a laboratory definition, and most such patients recover.

**Peak level at 1.5–2 h normally; within 4 hours in overdose — later with opioids, anticholinergics or food.** Anything that slows gastric emptying delays the peak, which is why a 4-hour level is the earliest valid one (APAP-06).
traps: “Toxicity is set by the number of tablets”
It is set by mg/kg — 10 g is far more dangerous in a 45 kg woman than in a 90 kg man.
“ALT 600 meets severe hepatotoxicity”
The definition is a peak above 1000 U/L.
decode: Minimum potentially toxic acute dose [pattern]
>150 mg/kg (7.5–10 g in an adult).
How is severe hepatotoxicity defined? [pattern]
Peak AST or ALT above 1000 U/L.
APAP-01.punch: Paracetamol is dosed by the liver’s capacity: above 150 mg/kg the safe pathways saturate and the toxic metabolite starts to win, and above 350 mg/kg it almost always wins unless N-acetylcysteine is given.
fix: WATCH: pesticides “dominate”
Pesticides dominate poisoning deaths in India, but acute liver failure in India is mostly viral hepatitis (HEV, HBV) and anti-TB drug injury.

APAP-02.sub: Toxicology → Dose & Mechanism → Metabolism and injury
APAP-02.intro: Paracetamol itself does not damage the liver; one of its metabolites does. Normally that metabolite is made in small amounts and neutralised at once by glutathione. Injury happens when the dose is large enough to use up glutathione, and it happens where the metabolite is made — around the central vein.
why: **90% glucuronidation and sulfation (non-toxic); 1–2% unchanged in urine; 5–9% oxidised (your notes’ text says 5–7%).** Of the conjugation routes, glucuronidation takes the larger share in adults, so it is the main reaction under normal conditions; sulfation is second. Conjugation attaches a water-soluble group so the drug can be excreted; the products are inert. Only the oxidised fraction is dangerous, and in overdose it grows because conjugation saturates.

**NAPQI (N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone imine), made by CYP2E1.** NAPQI is a reactive electrophile that attacks the sulphydryl groups of cell proteins. CYP2E1 is the main enzyme, with contributions from CYP3A4 and CYP1A2.

**Conjugation with glutathione to cysteine and mercapturic acid conjugates.** Glutathione donates its sulphydryl group to NAPQI, making a harmless conjugate excreted in urine. This handles only the small oxidised fraction — it is a rescue step, not a main route of metabolism.

**Injury begins when glutathione stores fall by 70–80%: NAPQI binds cell proteins (adducts), mitochondria fail, and the cell necroses.** While glutathione lasts, NAPQI is captured before it reaches proteins. Below about a quarter of normal, NAPQI binds mitochondrial proteins, ATP fails and the cell dies — so the mechanism of paracetamol liver failure is accumulation of NAPQI.

**Centrilobular (zone 3), where CYP450 is concentrated.** NAPQI is made where CYP2E1 is most abundant, around the central vein, so the necrosis is centrilobular and periportal (zone 1) cells are relatively spared.
traps: “The main pathway is CYP450 oxidation” or “conjugation to glutathione”
Under normal conditions the main reaction is glucuronidation; CYP oxidation is a 5–9% minor route and glutathione only detoxifies its product. 42% of the DocT cohort got this right.
“The toxic metabolite is made by glucuronidation”
Glucuronidation makes inert conjugates; NAPQI comes from CYP2E1 oxidation.
“Paracetamol injury is periportal”
It is centrilobular, zone 3 — where CYP2E1 is concentrated.
decode: Main reaction in paracetamol metabolism under normal conditions [DocT]
Conjugation to glucuronic acid — not CYP oxidation, not glutathione.
Analgesic overdose with liver failure: mechanism [Marrow]
Accumulation of NAPQI once glutathione is depleted.
Zone of necrosis [pattern]
Zone 3, centrilobular.
APAP-02.punch: Most paracetamol is glucuronidated harmlessly; only the small CYP2E1 fraction makes NAPQI, which glutathione neutralises until about three-quarters of the store is gone — and because CYP2E1 sits around the central vein, that is where the liver dies.

APAP-03.intro: Two things decide how much harm a given dose does: how fast NAPQI is made, and how much glutathione is there to meet it. Anything that speeds CYP oxidation or lowers glutathione raises the risk; anything that slows oxidation or boosts conjugation lowers it.
why: **Raises: chronic alcohol.** Long-term drinking induces CYP2E1, so more NAPQI is made from the same dose, and the poor nutrition that goes with it lowers glutathione. Both levers move against the patient — which is why injury can occur even at doses near or below the usual maximum.

**Raises: CYP inducers — anticonvulsants, antitubercular drugs — and tobacco.** Enzyme inducers increase oxidative metabolism. Isoniazid acts on CYP2E1; phenytoin, carbamazepine, phenobarbital and rifampicin induce other CYP isoforms that can also make NAPQI.

**Raises: fasting and malnutrition.** Glutathione is built from amino acids, chiefly cysteine; a malnourished patient has smaller stores and less capacity for conjugation, so NAPQI overwhelms the defence sooner.

**Raises: age over 40, Gilbert syndrome, repeated supratherapeutic dosing.** Older patients have less hepatic reserve. Gilbert syndrome reduces UGT1A1 activity, so less drug is glucuronidated (weak clinical evidence). Repeated dosing wears glutathione down over days (APAP-04).

**Lowers: childhood — more glutathione, more conjugation.** Children under about 10 clear paracetamol mainly by sulfation, whereas adults mainly glucuronidate; they sulfate efficiently and make glutathione readily, so less becomes NAPQI. The nomogram and NAC rules still apply to them.

**Lowers: acute alcohol co-ingestion — it competes for CYP2E1.** Ethanol drunk at the same time occupies CYP2E1, so less paracetamol is oxidised while the alcohol is present. The same enzyme, once induced by chronic drinking, has the opposite effect.
mimic: Acute vs chronic alcohol
Acute alcohol competes for CYP2E1 and protects; chronic alcohol induces CYP2E1 and depletes glutathione, and harms.
traps: “Young children metabolise paracetamol mainly by glucuronidation, like adults”
Under about 10 years sulfation is the predominant pathway; glucuronidation dominates only in adults. Only 31% of the DocT GT cohort got this right.
“Children are at higher risk because they are smaller”
Dosed per kg, children are at lower risk: more sulfation and glutathione.
“Alcohol always increases paracetamol toxicity”
Acute co-ingestion is protective; only chronic use increases risk.
“Risk factors mean a lower nomogram line in the UK”
The UK abolished its separate high-risk line in 2012; everyone is treated above the single 100 line (APAP-06).
decode: 3-year-old, 220 mg/kg: predominant pathway under 10 years [DocT GT]
Sulfation.
Chronic alcoholic, repeated supratherapeutic use: why higher risk? [DocT GT]
Increased CYP2E1 activity and low glutathione.
Chronic alcohol use disorder and overdose: most accurate statement [DocT]
Risk increased, even at doses below the usual safe limit.
APAP-03.punch: Every risk factor either makes more NAPQI or leaves less glutathione to meet it — which is why chronic alcohol harms, acute alcohol protects, and small children, who sulfate rather than glucuronidate, tolerate accidental doses best.
fix: Anticonvulsants listed as CYP2E1 inducers

Only isoniazid and alcohol act mainly on CYP2E1; phenytoin, carbamazepine, phenobarbital and rifampicin induce other CYP isoforms. The evidence that inducers raise risk is weak (the UK dropped its high-risk line in 2012).

APAP-04.sub: Toxicology → Dose & Mechanism → Repeated supratherapeutic ingestion
APAP-04.intro: Not every paracetamol poisoning is a single deliberate overdose. A patient in pain — a toothache, a fever — may take a little more than the maximum dose, several times a day, for several days. Each dose is small, but glutathione never recovers, and the patient comes in only once the liver is injured.
why: **More dangerous: presents late with established injury, so severe hepatotoxicity and death are more frequent.** There is no dramatic event to bring the patient in, so the treatment window passes unnoticed; such patients often have risk factors that lowered glutathione already (APAP-03). A young patient dosing every 4 hours for pain who turns up with ALT in the thousands is the typical picture — paracetamol is the drug to screen for.

**The nomogram does not apply: levels do not correlate with toxicity.** With many doses there is no single time zero, and much of the drug has already been metabolised, so a low level can coexist with severe injury.

**NAC if more than 7.5 g in 24 h (4 g with risk factors), symptoms, a level above 20 µg/mL, or raised transaminases (>50) whatever the level.** A level above 20 µg/mL means drug is still circulating to make NAPQI; a raised ALT means injury has begun. Dose thresholds differ between guidelines (Australia–NZ: 10 g or 200 mg/kg in 24 h, or 6 g or 150 mg/kg a day for 48 h or more), but the level and ALT triggers are shared.
mimic: Repeated ingestion vs staggered overdose
Both lack a single time zero, so neither can be plotted. A staggered overdose is several large doses over hours; repeated supratherapeutic ingestion is over-dosing for pain over days.
traps: “Plot the level and treat only if it is above the line”
The nomogram is invalid for repeated ingestion; treat on dose, level >20 or raised ALT.
“A low level means low risk”
The drug has already been metabolised; ALT tells you about injury.
decode: Teen taking an analgesic 4-hourly, ALT >2000: drug screen positive for [Marrow]
Paracetamol — repeated supratherapeutic ingestion.
Repeated ingestion, level 25 µg/mL, ALT normal [pattern]
Treat — a level above 20 is an indication.
APAP-04.punch: With repeated dosing there is no time zero to plot, the level understates the danger, and the patient comes late — so treatment is triggered by the dose, any meaningful level, or a rising ALT.
fix: Repeated ingestion: 7.5 g, or 4 g with risk factors, in 24 h

Guidelines use ≥10 g or 200 mg/kg in 24 h, or ≥6 g or 150 mg/kg a day for ≥48 h (US consensus 2006, Australia–NZ); Australia–NZ adds ≥4 g or 100 mg/kg in 24 h with risk factors. The level >20 µg/mL and ALT >50 triggers are right.

APAP-05.intro: Paracetamol poisoning unfolds over days, and the time course follows the mechanism. In the first day NAPQI is depleting glutathione but cells have not yet died, so the patient looks almost well. Necrosis declares itself on days 2 to 4, and those who survive the peak regenerate their liver.
why: **Stage I, 0.5–24 h: nausea, vomiting, pallor, sweating; laboratory tests usually normal.** Injury is under way inside the hepatocyte, but transaminases have not yet leaked — which is why a level is sent in every overdose (TOX-02).

**Stage II, 24–72 h: symptoms settle; right upper quadrant pain; transaminases rise; oliguria.** Hepatocytes are dying, so ALT and AST rise and the swollen liver is tender. Oliguria is the first sign of the renal tubular injury paracetamol can cause independently of the liver.

**Stage III, 72–96 h: peak injury — AST/ALT above 10,000, coagulopathy, hypoglycaemia, encephalopathy, lactic acidosis, AKI.** The failing liver cannot make clotting factors (INR rises), release glucose (hypoglycaemia is common and must be checked often), clear ammonia (encephalopathy) or clear lactate (lactic acidosis). Death is from cerebral oedema, dysrhythmias with multi-organ failure, haemorrhage or sepsis. The stage is set by the picture, not the clock: in severe poisoning jaundice, INR 3 and AKI at 36 h already mean fulminant failure, with these same killers.

**Stage IV, beyond 5 days: recovery, usually complete by day 7.** The liver regenerates from surviving cells and survivors usually recover without chronic liver disease, though histological recovery can take up to 3 months.
mimic: Stage I vs stage II vs fulminant failure
Nausea and sweating with normal enzymes is stage I; right upper quadrant tenderness with rising enzymes is stage II; jaundice, high INR and AKI is liver failure, whatever the hour.
traps: “At 36 hours with jaundice and INR 3, expect right upper quadrant tenderness (stage II)”
That is already fulminant failure; the associated complication is cerebral oedema and dysrhythmias. Only 31% of the DocT GT cohort got this right.
“Hypoglycaemia is rare in paracetamol liver failure” / “older or alcoholic patients do better”
Hypoglycaemia is common; age over 40 and chronic alcohol worsen prognosis. Lactic acidosis is the recognised complication.
“She feels better on day 2, so she can go home”
Stage II is the deceptive one: symptoms settle while the liver worsens. Decide on ALT and INR.
decode: 36 h after overdose: jaundice, INR 3.0, creatinine 2.5 — associated complication [DocT GT]
Cerebral oedema and dysrhythmias.
Paracetamol liver failure: which is true? [DocT]
Lactic acidosis is a recognised complication.
RUQ pain, rising enzymes at 48 h [pattern]

APAP-05.punch: The stages track the mechanism: silent glutathione depletion on day 1, necrosis the patient does not feel on day 2, liver failure by days 3–4 — or earlier if severe — and regeneration in survivors; so a well patient on day 2 is not a safe patient.
fix: Stage IV usually complete by day 7
Recovery runs from about day 4–5 to 2 weeks; the liver tissue takes up to 3 months to heal (Goldfrank’s).

APAP-06.intro: After a single overdose the paracetamol level falls steadily once absorption is complete. If the level at a known time is high, more drug is reaching CYP2E1 and the risk of injury is higher. The nomogram turns that into a line: plot one level against the hours since ingestion, and treat if the point lies above the line.
why: **It plots serum paracetamol against time since a single acute ingestion.** It is the risk tool for paracetamol (acetaminophen) only, and works only when there is one known time zero.

**Earliest valid level: 4 hours after ingestion.** Before 4 hours absorption may be incomplete, so the level is still rising and a low value can be falsely reassuring (APAP-01). A patient seen at 3 hours, even after a large dose, has the level taken at 4 hours: the result is back well inside the 8-hour window, so NAC can wait for it.

**Original line: 200 µg/mL at 4 h. Treatment line, 25% lower: 150 at 4 h.** The 200 line was drawn from patients who developed hepatotoxicity; US practice lowered it by 25% to allow for errors in timing and assay. Under this line, a valid 4-hour level decides — not the dose: 130 is below and not treated, 170 is above and treated.

**Revised UK line (2012): a single line from 100 at 4 h to 15 at 15 h, with no risk stratification.** The MHRA moved everyone to the 100 line because risk factors could not be judged reliably at the bedside (APAP-03); many more patients receive NAC.

**Not usable: staggered or repeated ingestion, unknown time; with sustained-release, take 4- and 8-hour levels and treat if either is above the line.** Without a single time zero the point cannot be placed; sustained-release tablets may give a late or second peak.
mimic: µg/mL vs mg/L vs mg/dL
µg/mL and mg/L are the same number (150 µg/mL = 150 mg/L); mg/dL would be 100 times larger, so a stem printing “130 mg/dL” means 130 µg/mL. In µmol/L multiply by about 6.6 (150 line ≈ 990 µmol/L).
traps: “100 tablets 3 hours ago: give NAC now” or “give charcoal 50 g”

Measure the 4-hour level in an hour — it will be back before 8 hours. Charcoal at 3 hours is outside the usual 1-hour window (UK; up to 2 h for large doses). DocT key; only 32% got it. Note the card conflict: APAP-08 allows charcoal to 4 hours, and Australia–NZ would give it for >30 g.
“Both took 15 g, so both get NAC”

DocT keys the US 150 line: 4-hour levels 130 (no NAC) and 170 (NAC). The stem’s “mg/dL” should read µg/mL; under the UK 100 line both would be treated, and many centres would treat 15 g on dose alone. Only 42% chose the key.
“The treatment line is 200 at 4 hours”
200 is the original line; the US treatment line is 150 and the UK line 100.
decode: Two patients, 15 g each, 4-hour levels 130 and 170: treatment [DocT]
Treat only the one above 150 (US line) — key; UK line would treat both.
17-year-old, 100 tablets 3 hours ago: next step [DocT]

Rumack–Matthew nomogram is used for which drug? [DocT GT]

APAP-06.punch: The nomogram reads one level against one time, so it needs a single ingestion at a known time and a level at 4 hours or later — then the only question is which line the question names: 200, 150 or 100.

APAP-07.intro: Some patients arrive in liver failure days after an overdose they do not mention. By then the paracetamol has been cleared, so the level is undetectable. But when NAPQI binds liver proteins and the cells die, the bound fragments leak into the blood and persist for days.
why: **They establish paracetamol as the cause of liver injury when the level is already undetectable.** Adducts form only when NAPQI binds protein cysteine groups (APAP-02), so they are specific, and they outlast the parent drug in blood.
**Above 1 nmol/mL (with ALT above 1000), measured by HPLC.** A high adduct level with severe hepatotoxicity indicates paracetamol caused the injury; therapeutic dosing gives only low levels.
**AcetaSTAT: a competitive immunoassay giving a positive or negative result only.** A rapid bedside strip test where HPLC is not available; it does not give a number.
mimic: Paracetamol level vs adducts
The level measures drug still in the blood and guides NAC early; adducts measure injury already done and identify the cause late.
traps: “An undetectable level excludes paracetamol as the cause of liver failure”
The drug is cleared within a day; adducts persist and can prove the cause.
decode: Acute liver failure, denies overdose, paracetamol undetectable: confirmatory test [pattern]
Paracetamol–protein adducts.
APAP-07.punch: When the drug has gone but the liver has failed, adducts are the fingerprint NAPQI left on the dead cells — proof of cause, not a guide to NAC dosing.

APAP-08.intro: The liver cannot take up glutathione given from outside, but it can make its own from cysteine. N-acetylcysteine delivers that cysteine, so it refills the store that NAPQI is draining. Its effect is greatest before glutathione runs out — but it still helps after that.
why: **Replenishes glutathione; enhances sulfation; antioxidant and anti-inflammatory.** NAC is deacetylated to cysteine, the rate-limiting building block of glutathione, so NAPQI is captured before it reaches proteins. Once injury has started, its antioxidant action and improved microcirculation limit further damage — the reason it helps even in liver failure.

**Within 8 hours of ingestion: near-complete protection.** In the first 8 hours glutathione has not yet fallen to the point at which NAPQI binds proteins (APAP-02). After that each hour of delay allows more necrosis — so a patient already beyond 8 hours after a toxic dose gets NAC at once, before the level is back.

**Activated charcoal 1 g/kg (maximum 50 g) within 4 hours of a single ingestion; not with altered sensorium unless the airway is protected.** The usual window is 1 hour (TOX-09; UK up to 2 hours for large doses); Australia–NZ extends it to 4 hours only for very large (>30 g) or modified-release ingestions.
mimic: NAC before vs after 8 hours
Before 8 hours it prevents injury by refilling glutathione; after 8 hours it limits injury that has begun, so it is started immediately.
traps: “Pinpoint pupils after codeine + 30 g paracetamol at 12 h: naloxone first”

With BP held and no respiratory depression described, the time-critical treatment is NAC — already past 8 hours after a massive dose. Naloxone is for depressed breathing or consciousness (and precipitates withdrawal in an IV drug user); flumazenil has no role. Only 45% chose NAC.
“After 8 hours NAC is useless”
It is still given late and in established liver failure; it improves outcome.
“NAC works by binding paracetamol”
It replenishes glutathione, which binds NAPQI.
decode: 12 h after 480 mg codeine + 30 g paracetamol, BP 100/60, pinpoint pupils: most appropriate [DocT]
Start N-acetylcysteine.
Main mechanism of NAC [pattern]
Replenishes glutathione.
APAP-08.punch: NAC refills the glutathione that NAPQI drains: given within 8 hours it prevents injury almost completely, and given later it still limits the damage — so a late presenter gets it at once, ahead of the level and ahead of the distractions.
fix: Charcoal within 4 hours
The usual window is 1 hour; Australia–NZ uses 2 hours for a toxic dose and up to 4 hours only for >30 g or modified-release tablets.

APAP-09.intro: NAC can be given intravenously over about a day or by mouth over three days. Both aim to keep glutathione ahead of NAPQI until the paracetamol has been cleared; they differ in route, length and side effects.
why: **IV 21-hour protocol: bag 1 150 mg/kg in 200 mL 5% dextrose over 60 min; bag 2 50 mg/kg in 500 mL over 4 h; bag 3 100 mg/kg in 1000 mL over 16 h — 300 mg/kg in total.** The large first dose refills glutathione quickly while NAPQI production peaks; the later bags (12.5 then 6.25 mg/kg/h) keep it topped up while the drug clears.
**Oral protocol: 140 mg/kg, then 70 mg/kg every 4 h for 17 doses (72 hours).** Oral NAC goes straight to the liver through the portal vein, but the taste and vomiting make doses hard to keep down.
**IV is chosen for vomiting, no oral route, pregnancy and liver failure.** In all of these the oral dose may not be absorbed or tolerated, and reliable delivery matters most.

**Main adverse effect of IV: an anaphylactoid reaction — rate-related, not IgE — so slow or pause, give an antihistamine, then restart.** NAC releases histamine directly, mostly during the concentrated first bag. No antibody is involved, so it is not a contraindication.
traps: “A rash on bag 1 means NAC must be stopped for good”
It is anaphylactoid: pause, antihistamine, restart.
“The oral course lasts 21 hours”
Oral is 72 hours (loading dose plus 17 doses); IV is 21 hours.
decode: Flushing and wheeze 30 minutes into IV NAC [pattern]
Anaphylactoid reaction — pause, antihistamine, restart.
Total IV NAC dose and duration [pattern]
300 mg/kg over 21 hours.
APAP-09.punch: Both regimens refill glutathione — IV front-loads it over 21 hours, oral spreads it over 72 — and the IV reaction is anaphylactoid, so it means slowing down, not stopping.

parts.q: Newer IV regimens with fewer reactions?
parts.a: **SNAP**: 100 mg/kg over 2 h, then 200 mg/kg over 10 h; **two-bag**: 200 mg/kg over 4 h, then 100 mg/kg over 16 h. Both give 300 mg/kg without the concentrated first bag, so fewer reactions.

APAP-10.intro: The 21-hour protocol is a fixed course, but the patient may not be finished when the bags are. NAC is needed for as long as paracetamol is still being turned into NAPQI or the liver is still being injured. So the decision to stop rests on blood tests — liver function tests among them — rather than the clock.
why: **Stop when paracetamol is undetectable, ALT is falling, and INR is below 2.** No drug means no more NAPQI; a falling ALT means necrosis has stopped; an INR under 2 means synthetic function is preserved. This is why LFTs and INR are taken at presentation and again before NAC ends in every paracetamol overdose.
**If not met at 21 hours, continue at 6.25 mg/kg/h — the third-bag rate — and repeat the tests 12-hourly.** Continuing at that rate maintains protection without a new loading dose.
**In established liver failure, continue until transplant or resolution.** NAC still improves survival once the liver is failing (APAP-08).
mimic: Falling ALT: recovery vs burnout
A falling ALT with a falling INR means recovery; a falling ALT with a rising INR means too few hepatocytes are left (APAP-11).
traps: “NAC should routinely be given to anyone presenting within 12 hours”
Within 8 hours NAC is guided by the 4-hour level on the nomogram (APAP-06), not given routinely; the statement that holds is that LFTs must be monitored. Only 57% chose it.
“Over the age of 6, she is unlikely to develop significant toxicity”
Only young children are relatively protected (sulfation, APAP-03); a 19-year-old is an adult.
“The 21-hour course is complete, so stop NAC”
Stop only if the level is undetectable, ALT falling and INR below 2.
decode: 19-year-old with paracetamol overdose: which statement is correct? [DocT]
Liver function tests should be monitored.
End of 21 h: level undetectable, ALT rising, INR 2.4 [pattern]
Continue NAC at 6.25 mg/kg/h, repeat tests in 12 hours.
APAP-10.punch: NAC is stopped by the blood tests, not the clock: when no drug is left, the ALT is falling and the INR is under 2 — otherwise it continues at the third-bag rate.

APAP-11.sub: Toxicology → Transplant & Sweep → King’s College criteria
APAP-11.intro: Most patients with paracetamol liver failure recover with NAC and intensive care, but some will die without a transplant. King’s College criteria pick out that group using markers of how much liver function is left. Transaminases are not among them: they measure how many cells died, not how many survive.
why: **Arterial pH below 7.30 after fluid resuscitation; OR all three of creatinine above 3.4 mg/dL, grade 3 or 4 encephalopathy and INR above 6.5 (PT above 100 s).** Persistent acidosis means the liver cannot clear lactate and other acids; pH alone is enough. INR measures synthetic function, encephalopathy detoxification, and creatinine the renal injury. A patient who meets them needs emergency transplant evaluation, not more enzymes or observation.
**Specificity 90%, sensitivity only 60%: it misses patients who will die.** When the criteria are met, death without transplant is very likely; failing to meet them is not reassurance.

**Lactate modification: above 3.5 after 1 hour of fluid resuscitation, or above 3.0 after adequate fluids.** Units are mmol/L; in the original study (Bernal 2002) the early value was taken about 4 hours after admission and the later one at about 12 hours, after full resuscitation — not at 1 hour. The necrotic liver both fails to clear lactate and produces it, so lactic acidosis is a recognised complication and adding lactate identifies non-survivors earlier.
mimic: Paracetamol vs non-paracetamol criteria

Non-paracetamol King’s use INR >6.5 alone, or three of five (age <10 or >40, aetiology, jaundice-to-encephalopathy >7 days, INR >3.5, bilirubin >17.5 mg/dL). Factor V <20–30% with encephalopathy is the Clichy criterion. Age, bilirubin and factor V are distractors in a paracetamol question.
traps: “ALT (or the paracetamol level) at 30 hours best predicts outcome”
ALT measures injury, not outcome; among ALT, bilirubin, creatinine and level, creatinine is the King’s marker. DocT keys ALT — disputed; the card is right. 58% chose the key.
“Not meeting King’s criteria means the patient will survive”
Sensitivity is only about 60%.
“A falling ALT means recovery”
With a rising INR it means too little liver is left.
decode: pH 7.25, creatinine 3.8, INR 7.2, grade III: which finding alone predicts poor prognosis? [DocT GT]
Arterial pH <7.3.
pH 7.25, INR 7.0, creatinine 3.8, grade IV: next best step [DocT GT]
Emergency liver transplant evaluation.
30 h after 25 g: test most helpful for outcome [DocT]
Key ALT (disputed); by King’s, creatinine.
APAP-11.punch: King’s College criteria measure what the liver can no longer do — clear acid, make clotting factors, protect the brain and the kidneys — so they predict death well when met, but miss many who will still die.

APAP-12.sub: Toxicology → Transplant & Sweep → Adjuncts in massive overdose
APAP-12.intro: In a massive overdose NAC alone may not keep up, and enormous levels can poison mitochondria directly, giving coma and lactic acidosis within hours. Adjuncts either stop NAPQI being made or remove the drug — always on top of NAC, never in place of it.
why: **Fomepizole: a CYP2E1 inhibitor, an emerging adjunct to NAC (case reports).** Blocking CYP2E1 cuts NAPQI formation at its source; human evidence is limited to case reports.

**Haemodialysis clears paracetamol; it is used in massive ingestion with severe lactic acidosis, and is never a substitute for NAC.** Paracetamol is small, poorly protein-bound and has a modest volume of distribution, so dialysis removes it. EXTRIP (2014) recommends it for a level >1000 mg/L without NAC, or mitochondrial dysfunction (coma, acidosis, raised lactate) with a level >700 mg/L without NAC or >900 mg/L with NAC. NAC continues at a higher rate, because dialysis removes it too.
**Cimetidine worked in animals but gave no benefit in humans.** A CYP inhibitor in theory; no clinical benefit, so no role.
mimic: Early vs late acidosis in paracetamol poisoning
Early (hours), with coma and a massive level, is mitochondrial toxicity — consider dialysis. Late (days 3–4) is liver failure — a King’s criterion (APAP-11).
traps: “Dialysis can replace NAC in massive overdose”
It is always added to NAC, never instead of it.
decode: Massive ingestion, comatose, severe lactic acidosis, level 950 mg/L on NAC [pattern]
Haemodialysis plus NAC at an increased rate.
APAP-12.punch: In a massive overdose the adjuncts attack the same problem from two ends — fomepizole stops NAPQI being made, dialysis removes the drug — but NAC stays the treatment throughout.

APAP-13.sub: Toxicology → Transplant & Sweep → True or false
APAP-13.intro: This card tests the deck’s key distinctions. Each statement either holds or turns on one detail from an earlier card; the reason is the mechanism you met there.
why: **False — the toxic metabolite is formed by CYP2E1 oxidation.** Glucuronidation makes inert conjugates; NAPQI comes from the small oxidised fraction (APAP-02).
**False — injury is centrilobular.** CYP2E1 is concentrated in zone 3, so NAPQI is made, and cells die, around the central vein (APAP-02).
**False — the level must be taken at 4 hours or later.** Before 4 hours absorption may be incomplete and the level still rising (APAP-06).
**False — acute alcohol is protective; chronic alcohol harms.** Acute ethanol competes for CYP2E1; chronic use induces it and lowers glutathione (APAP-03).
**True — the US treatment line starts at 150 at 4 hours,** 25% below the original 200 line as a safety margin (APAP-06).
**True — the first IV NAC bag is 150 mg/kg,** to refill glutathione quickly (APAP-09).
**True — NAC is stopped when INR is below 2 and ALT falling, with an undetectable level.** All three are needed: no drug left, necrosis over, function preserved (APAP-10).
**True — pH below 7.30 after fluids meets King’s criteria** on its own (APAP-11).
traps: “Alcohol increases toxicity”
Only chronic alcohol; acute co-ingestion protects.
“INR <2 and falling ALT are enough to stop NAC”
The level must also be undetectable.
decode: Chronic alcoholic, repeated supratherapeutic use: why higher risk? [DocT GT]
Increased CYP2E1 activity and low glutathione — not renal clearance or absorption.
True/false on metabolism or the nomogram [pattern]
Ask which pathway makes NAPQI (CYP2E1) and which time and line apply (≥4 h; 200, 150, 100).
APAP-13.punch: Every statement here turns on a mechanism from earlier in the deck — CYP2E1 making NAPQI in zone 3, absorption complete by 4 hours, and stopping or listing decided by what the liver can still do.

APAP-14.sub: Toxicology → Transplant & Sweep → Indications for NAC
APAP-14.intro: NAC is safe and the cost of missing paracetamol toxicity is a dead liver, so the indications are deliberately broad. They follow one logic: treat whenever the nomogram says the dose is toxic, whenever it cannot be used but toxicity is possible, and whenever the liver is already injured.
why: **Single ingestion with a level at 4 hours or later above the treatment line.** A known time and a valid level place the patient in the risk zone (APAP-06).

**More than 150 mg/kg (7.5 g) with no level available within 8 hours.** Protection is near-complete only if NAC starts within 8 hours (APAP-08), so waiting for a late result throws away the window — and a patient who arrives after 8 hours with a toxic dose gets NAC immediately. Stop if the level returns below the line.
**Unknown dose or time with a level above 10 µg/mL.** Without a time the level cannot be plotted, so any measurable paracetamol means drug is still present to form NAPQI.
**Any ingestion with evidence of liver injury.** A raised ALT shows NAPQI has already overwhelmed glutathione, whatever the level or history.
**Presentation after 24 hours with liver injury.** The nomogram ends at 24 hours, but NAC still improves outcome in late presenters (APAP-08).
mimic: Acute single vs repeated supratherapeutic ingestion
Acute: these indications and the nomogram. Repeated: dose, level >20 or raised ALT (APAP-04).
traps: “Mixed overdose with a striking other finding (opioid pupils, long QTc after ecstasy): treat that first”
Suspect hidden paracetamol in any analgesic overdose with vomiting; when the time and dose make it toxic, NAC is the answer the question wants.
“No paracetamol in the history, so no level”
Send a level in every deliberate overdose: co-ingestion is common and stage I looks harmless.
“NAC routinely for everyone presenting within 12 hours”
Within 8 hours, wait for the 4-hour level and use the nomogram; LFTs are monitored in all (APAP-10).
decode: Ecstasy, peptic ulcer, analgesic use, vomiting, QTc 503: next step [Marrow]
N-acetylcysteine — hidden paracetamol.
12 h after codeine + 30 g paracetamol, pinpoint pupils [DocT]
Start NAC.
19-year-old overdose: correct statement [DocT]
LFTs should be monitored — not routine NAC within 12 h.
APAP-14.punch: NAC is given whenever toxicity is shown, cannot be ruled out in time, or has already begun — because the drug is safe and the window is short.

PEST-01.sub: Toxicology → Pesticides → Scale and WHO hazard classes
PEST-01.intro: Organophosphates are the single biggest cause of fatal poisoning in the developing world, because they are cheap, sold without control and kept in the homes of farming families. Most deaths are deliberate self-poisoning. The WHO grades the compounds by how little of them kills a rat, which is the only practical way of saying in advance how dangerous a bottle is.
why: **About 3 million people exposed and up to 300,000 deaths a year; the commonest poisoning in developing countries.** In India poisoning is predominantly rural and agricultural, and organophosphates are among its commonest causes. Case fatality — of the order of 10–20% in South Asian series — is far higher than in Western data, because the dose swallowed is large, the hospital is far and ventilation is scarce.

**Class Ia extremely hazardous, oral LD50 <5 mg/kg; Ib highly hazardous 5–50; II moderately hazardous 50–2000; III slightly hazardous >2000; U unlikely to be hazardous ≥5000.** The LD50 is the single oral dose that kills half of a group of rats, so the lower the LD50, the higher the hazard.
mimic: WHO hazard class vs clinical severity
Class reflects intrinsic toxicity. Severity in the patient is set by the amount, formulation and delay, and is graded by RBC cholinesterase activity (PEST-09).
traps: “Poisoning, and pesticide poisoning, are mainly urban; mortality matches Western data”
In India both are mainly rural, and mortality is much higher than in the West.
“A high WHO class number means a more dangerous pesticide”
It is the reverse: Ia is the most hazardous and III the least.
decode: Epidemiology of poisoning in India: most accurate statement [DocT]
Organophosphates are a common cause — not urban predominance, not Western-level mortality.
“Oral LD50 <5 mg/kg” — WHO class? [pattern]
Class Ia, extremely hazardous.
PEST-01.punch: The WHO class is only the compound’s intrinsic toxicity read backwards from its LD50 — the reason organophosphates kill so many in rural India is availability and dose, not subtlety.
fix: Up to 300,000 deaths a year from organophosphates
About 250,000–370,000 deaths a year are from all pesticide self-poisoning, organophosphates the largest share.

PEST-02.intro: All organophosphates do the same thing to acetylcholinesterase, so the class matters for two other reasons: the alkyl side groups decide how quickly the enzyme–poison bond becomes permanent, and fat solubility decides how long the illness lasts. Carbamates give the same clinical picture with different chemistry. Nerve agents are the military members of the organophosphate family — and are treated the same way.
why: **Dimethyl: dichlorvos, fenthion, malathion, methamidophos.** The bound enzyme loses a methyl group fast, so ageing takes only about 3 hours (PEST-03) and the window for an oxime is short.

**Diethyl: chlorpyrifos, diazinon, parathion, quinalphos.** Ethyl groups are lost slowly, so ageing takes about 33 hours and oximes still work the next day. Parathion poisoning is the classic organophosphate crisis treated with atropine plus pralidoxime. Several (chlorpyrifos, parathion) are thions needing hepatic activation, so onset can be delayed and prolonged.
**Atypical: profenofos.** Its side chains fit neither pattern and the enzyme it inhibits is poorly reactivatable, so oximes do little for it.

**Nerve agents: sarin, tabun, soman, VX.** Chemical-warfare organophosphates, far more potent and absorbed through skin and lungs. The toxidrome is the same muscarinic flood — miosis, bradycardia, tears, salivation, diarrhoea, urination — and so are the antidotes: atropine plus pralidoxime, given early because soman ages within minutes.
**Carbamates: carbaryl, aldicarb, methomyl, propoxur.** They carbamylate the same site but the bond hydrolyses spontaneously, so there is no ageing and the illness is shorter (PEST-03).
mimic: Lipophilic vs water-soluble organophosphate
Fenthion and malathion are stored in fat and leach back out, so cholinergic features relapse; water-soluble agents give one defined illness.
Nerve agent vs anticholinergic plant vs cyanide
Sarin: wet, miotic, bradycardic — atropine + pralidoxime. Atropa belladonna: dry, dilated, hot — physostigmine. Cyanide: hydroxocobalamin.
traps: “Ethanol for isopropyl alcohol, glucagon for cocaine, D5 for methaemoglobinaemia”

None is a recognised antidote: isopropanol makes acetone, so ADH blockade is pointless; glucagon is for β-blocker and calcium-channel-blocker poisoning; methaemoglobinaemia needs methylene blue. Pralidoxime in sarin is the recognised one — only 43% chose it in one sitting.
“Sarin needs atropine alone” or “a different antidote”
Severe nerve-agent poisoning gets atropine and pralidoxime, as for any organophosphate.
“Aldicarb is an organophosphate”
Aldicarb is a carbamate (and WHO class Ia); parathion is the diethyl organophosphate.
decode: Recognised treatment option in poisoning (vs ethanol–isopropanol, glucagon–cocaine, D5–methaemoglobin) [DocT]
Pralidoxime in sarin poisoning.
Subway release of sarin, most severe patients: best management [DocT GT]
Atropine and pralidoxime.
Villagers: diarrhoea, urination, tears, bradycardia, miosis, salivation [DocT GT]
Sarin; atropine and pralidoxime.
Cholinergic crisis treated with atropine + pralidoxime: agent [Marrow]
Parathion (diethyl OP), not aldicarb (carbamate).
PEST-02.punch: The subclass tells you nothing new about the toxidrome and everything about the clock: dimethyl ages in hours, diethyl in a day and a half, soman in minutes, carbamates never — and every organophosphate, nerve agents included, gets atropine plus an oxime.

PEST-03.intro: Acetylcholinesterase splits acetylcholine the instant it is released. An organophosphate leaves a phosphate group stuck on its catalytic (esteratic) site, so transmitter accumulates at muscarinic, nicotinic and central synapses. At first that phosphate can still be pulled off; after a chemical rearrangement — ageing — it cannot.
why: **Phosphorylates the esteratic site of acetylcholinesterase, so acetylcholine accumulates at muscarinic, nicotinic and CNS synapses.** This is conventionally called irreversible inhibition: the phosphorylated enzyme does not recover on its own in any useful time, unlike a carbamylated one. Strictly, it is slowly reversible by an oxime until it ages, and only then truly permanent.

**Loss of an alkyl group from the bound enzyme: the bond becomes irreversible and oximes no longer work.** The aged enzyme carries a stable, negatively charged phosphate an oxime cannot attack; recovery then depends on new enzyme, over weeks.
**Dimethyl about 3 hours; diethyl about 33 hours.** Half-lives of ageing. The smaller methyl group leaves far more readily, hence the tenfold difference.

**A dimethyl patient arriving at 3 hours already has half the enzyme aged, so oximes work far better in diethyl poisoning; profenofos ages faster still.** An oxime is still worth giving a day later after chlorpyrifos, and it is started while the compound is unknown.

**Carbamylation is reversible, with no ageing; shorter illness; little CNS penetration.** The carbamyl–enzyme bond hydrolyses within hours, so the enzyme recovers without an antidote; carbamates cross the blood–brain barrier poorly.
mimic: Organophosphate vs carbamate at the bedside
Identical cholinergic syndrome; carbamate illness resolves in a day or two, rarely shows the intermediate syndrome, and needs atropine but not an oxime.
traps: “Organophosphates cause reversible inhibition of AChE” / “block ACh receptors” / “release ACh”
The keyed answer is irreversible inhibition of acetylcholinesterase; reversible inhibition is the carbamate. Only 58% got it right.
“Ageing is faster with diethyl compounds”
The opposite: dimethyl ~3 h, diethyl ~33 h.
“Carbamates need no treatment”
They need atropine and often ventilation; what they do not need is an oxime.
decode: Primary biochemical effect of organophosphates [DocT]
Irreversible inhibition of acetylcholinesterase.
“Oximes would be least useful in poisoning with…” [pattern]
A dimethyl compound or profenofos.
PEST-03.punch: Organophosphate inhibition is called irreversible because it becomes so once the enzyme ages — fast in dimethyl and profenofos, slow in diethyl — while carbamate inhibition is reversible and never ages.

PEST-04.intro: Everything in cholinergic poisoning follows from where acetylcholine receptors sit. Muscarinic receptors are on glands, smooth muscle and the heart’s pacemaker; nicotinic receptors are at the neuromuscular junction and in autonomic ganglia; both are in the brain. So the patient shows glandular flooding and bradycardia, weakness and sometimes tachycardia, and coma and loss of respiratory drive.
why: **Muscarinic — salivation, lacrimation, urination, diarrhoea, GI cramps, emesis; bradycardia, bronchorrhoea, bronchospasm; miosis.** Every exocrine gland is turned on — including sweat glands, so the skin is wet — and smooth muscle contracts. The patient is wet, miotic and bradycardic, often frothing at the mouth; a hot, dry patient is anticholinergic (or over-atropinised), not cholinergic. Bronchorrhoea flooding the alveoli, raised capillary permeability and aspiration give bilateral infiltrates with a normal heart and CVP — non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema. Atropine blocks these effects (PEST-10).

**Nicotinic — fasciculation, weakness, paralysis; tachycardia, hypertension, mydriasis from ganglionic stimulation.** Persistent acetylcholine first makes muscle twitch, then depolarises the end-plate into a block, so fasciculation gives way to flaccid weakness, including the diaphragm. Atropine does nothing here; fasciculation or weakness persisting after atropine is the sign that an oxime is needed (PEST-11).

**CNS — confusion, coma, convulsions; central respiratory depression.** Lipophilic organophosphates cross into the brain and finally depress the brainstem respiratory centre. The commonest cause of death is respiratory failure — bronchorrhoea and bronchospasm, nicotinic diaphragm failure and central apnoea together — not cardiotoxicity.
mimic: Organophosphate vs other garden poisons
Small pupils, bradycardia and frothing are cholinergic; paraquat gives caustic mouth and later lung fibrosis, glyphosate GI injury and shock, creosote phenol burns — none is miotic and wet.
Bilateral infiltrates: non-cardiogenic oedema vs ARDS
Both have a normal CVP. DocT keys ‘non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema’ as the umbrella term; if the stem gives Berlin criteria it is ARDS and gets lung-protective ventilation.
traps: “Hyperthermia is expected in cholinergic crisis”
It is the least expected feature: the patient sweats and is wet. Hyperthermia points to an anticholinergic state or atropine toxicity. Only 58% chose it.
“Bilateral infiltrates with normal heart size and CVP — ARDS” (or aspiration)
DocT keys non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema (50% right); ARDS is defensible by Berlin, aspiration is one contributor.
“Persisting bronchorrhoea or miosis after atropine means pralidoxime is needed”
Those are muscarinic — give more atropine. Fasciculation is the nicotinic sign that calls for the oxime.
“Tachycardia excludes organophosphate poisoning”
Ganglionic stimulation, hypoxia and bronchospasm all raise the rate.
decode: Agricultural worker, wet, miotic, bradycardic: least expected feature [DocT]
Hyperthermia.
Intubated OP patient, bilateral infiltrates, normal heart and CVP [DocT]
Non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema (ARDS defensible).
After atropine, which finding indicates pralidoxime? [NEET 2025]
Muscle fasciculations.
75-year-old found in garden: unconscious, small pupils, HR 50, frothing [DocT]
Organophosphorus poisoning.
PEST-04.punch: Read the patient receptor by receptor: glands and airway are muscarinic and answer to atropine, muscle and ganglia are nicotinic and answer only to an oxime, and the brain adds coma and apnoea — which is why these patients die of their airway, not their heart.
