PEST-05.intro: Weakness in organophosphate poisoning comes in three waves with different mechanisms: day one, day three, and weeks later. Only the first responds to atropine, the second needs a ventilator and nothing else, and the third is a neuropathy that no antidote touches. The clock after exposure is the main discriminator.
why: **Type I — acute cholinergic crisis: minutes to hours, generalised weakness with fasciculation, responds to atropine.** The cholinergic flood itself (PEST-04); atropine reverses the muscarinic half, which saves the airway.

**Type II — intermediate syndrome: 24–96 hours, neck flexors, proximal limb, cranial nerve and respiratory muscles, no response to atropine.** It appears after the crisis has settled, in a conscious, afebrile patient who looked to be recovering — a post-synaptic nicotinic problem (PEST-06).

**Type III — delayed neuropathy (OPIDN): 1–3 weeks, distal muscles, legs first, ascending, no response to atropine.** A dying-back axonopathy from inhibition of neuropathy target esterase, not acetylcholinesterase (PEST-07) — so neither persistent AChE inhibition nor antibodies explain it.
mimic: Intermediate syndrome vs myasthenic crisis vs Guillain–Barré
All give respiratory weakness; the intermediate syndrome follows a documented cholinergic crisis by 1–4 days, with neck-flexor weakness, intact sensation and no antibodies.
OPIDN vs intermediate syndrome
Distal and sensory at 1–3 weeks versus proximal, neck-flexor and respiratory at 24–96 hours.
traps: “Weakness and areflexia 7 days after OP: persistent AChE inhibition or myositis”
DocT keys OPIDP (neuropathy target esterase) for this delayed complication. Note the stem’s ‘proximal’ weakness fits poorly — the textbook OPIDN is distal and ascending.
“Intermediate syndrome affects distal muscles first”
It is neck flexors and proximal muscles; distal weakness is the delayed neuropathy.
“Recovery from the crisis means the patient can be extubated and discharged”
The intermediate syndrome begins exactly then — keep ventilation available for 4 days.
decode: 48 h after atropine + pralidoxime: neck flexor weakness, respiratory distress, afebrile, conscious [DocT]
Intermediate syndrome — not myasthenic crisis, GBS or neuropathy.
72 h later: neck flexor weakness, shallow breathing [DocT GT]
Intermediate syndrome.
7 days later: weakness, areflexia, prolonged ventilation — mechanism [DocT]
OPIDP (neuropathy target esterase).
PEST-05.punch: Three waves, three mechanisms: the cholinergic flood answers to atropine, the intermediate syndrome answers only to a ventilator, and the delayed neuropathy belongs to a different enzyme altogether.

PEST-06.intro: In a substantial minority the cholinergic crisis settles, atropine is weaned, and then over a few hours the patient cannot hold the head up, cannot cough and stops breathing adequately. Nothing prevents it and nothing shortens it; what matters is that a ventilator is ready.
why: **10–40% of patients; 24–96 hours after exposure, after the cholinergic crisis has resolved.** The timing is the point: it begins when the muscarinic features have gone and the patient appears to be improving.

**Neck flexion weakness (cannot lift the head off the pillow), proximal limb weakness, cranial nerve palsies, reduced reflexes, respiratory failure.** Neck flexors, girdle muscles, facial and bulbar muscles and the diaphragm fail; distal strength and sensation are preserved (PEST-07), and there are no recurrent muscarinic signs.
**Highly fat-soluble agents; possibly inadequate oxime dosing.** Lipophilic compounds such as fenthion keep releasing poison from fat (PEST-02); whether too little oxime contributes is debated.

**Persistent nicotinic over-stimulation with receptor down-regulation and muscle necrosis.** Continuous acetylcholine at the end-plate desensitises and down-regulates post-synaptic receptors and damages muscle fibres. Because the problem is post-synaptic and structural, neither atropine nor an oxime alters it.
**Supportive ventilation; no treatment prevents it.** Recovery takes days to weeks. Watch head lift, single-breath count and vital capacity, and intubate before the patient tires.
mimic: Intermediate syndrome vs recurrent cholinergic crisis
Returning secretions, wheeze and miosis is cholinergic and needs atropine; pure weakness with a dry chest is the intermediate syndrome.
Intermediate syndrome vs myasthenic crisis
Same proximal, bulbar and respiratory pattern; the poisoning history and preceding cholinergic phase decide it.
traps: “It is a rebound cholinergic crisis, so give more atropine”
Without muscarinic signs it is nicotinic and post-synaptic; atropine does not treat it.
“Atropine toxicity explains the weakness” / “it was a carbamate”
Atropine excess gives a hot, dry, delirious patient, not paralysis; carbamates rarely cause the intermediate syndrome.
“The patient is well at 24 hours, so discharge”
This is the window in which the syndrome begins; observe for at least 4 days.
decode: Improved with atropine, then progressive weakness and respiratory failure [DocT / DocT GT]
Intermediate syndrome — not rebound crisis, atropine toxicity or carbamate.
Day 3: cannot lift head, proximal and facial weakness, no muscarinic signs [DocT GT]
Intermediate syndrome.
48–72 h, neck flexor weakness and shallow breathing [DocT / DocT GT]
Intermediate syndrome.
PEST-06.punch: The intermediate syndrome is the trap of the second and third day: the cholinergic storm is over, the antidote is being weaned, and the only treatment for the weakness that follows is a ventilator you decided on early.

PEST-07.intro: Weeks after the poisoning is over, some patients return with numb feet and a slapping gait. This has nothing to do with acetylcholinesterase: certain organophosphates inhibit another esterase in the axon, and the long nerves degenerate from their tips backwards. Because the mechanism is separate, so are the timing, the pattern and the irrelevance of the acute severity.
why: **Inhibition of neuropathy target esterase, not acetylcholinesterase.** The compound phosphorylates this axonal enzyme, which then ages; the modified enzyme triggers a dying-back degeneration of the longest axons. So the mechanism of a delayed weakness is not persistent AChE inhibition, and cholinergic antidotes are irrelevant.

**Stocking-and-glove paraesthesia, then distal flaccid weakness of the legs ascending to the arms; absent ankle jerks.** The longest fibres fail first, sensory before motor, with wasting and areflexia; some patients are left with spasticity.
**Chlorpyrifos is the typical agent.** It is the compound in common agricultural use most often reported; triorthocresyl phosphate is the historical one.

**Independent of the severity of the acute poisoning: it can follow a mild acute illness.** The two enzymes have different sensitivities, so a compound can inhibit neuropathy target esterase while causing only modest cholinergic symptoms.
**Carbamates only rarely cause it.** They inhibit neuropathy target esterase weakly and the bond does not age.
mimic: OPIDN vs Guillain–Barré syndrome
Both ascend; OPIDN starts 1–3 weeks after a known exposure and progresses over days to weeks.
traps: “Delayed weakness is persistent AChE inhibition at the junction” or “antibody-mediated”
It is OPIDP — neuropathy target esterase. 71% got it right.
“Delayed neuropathy follows only severe poisoning”
It is independent of acute severity.
“Pralidoxime given early prevents it”
Oximes act on acetylcholinesterase, not neuropathy target esterase.
decode: Weakness, areflexia and ventilator dependence ~7 days after OP: mechanism [DocT]
Organophosphate-induced delayed polyneuropathy.
Three weeks after chlorpyrifos: numb feet, foot drop, absent ankle jerks [pattern]
OPIDN.
PEST-07.punch: OPIDN is organophosphate poisoning in a different enzyme: a dying-back axonopathy of the longest nerves that arrives weeks later, ignores how ill the patient was, and has no antidote.

PEST-08.sub: Toxicology → Pesticides → Delayed manifestations by time
PEST-08.intro: Organophosphate poisoning is a sequence spread over three weeks, and most of it appears after the patient has been declared out of danger. The order follows the mechanisms: continuing absorption first, then the neuromuscular junction, then the brain, and last the peripheral axon.
why: **Delayed-onset cholinergic phase at 40–48 hours.** With lipophilic and thion compounds poison keeps arriving at the synapse, so secretions and miosis return; it responds to atropine.
**Intermediate syndrome at 24–96 hours.** Nicotinic failure of neck flexors, proximal, bulbar and respiratory muscles, needing ventilation (PEST-06).
**Late-onset intermediate syndrome at about 114 hours.** The same syndrome beyond four days, typically with fat-soluble agents.
**Delayed encephalopathy or coma at 4–6 days.** Confusion or coma after the acute phase, with no new muscarinic signs.
**Cerebellar ataxia at about 8 days.** Usually self-limiting.
**Extrapyramidal syndrome at 5–15 days.** Dystonia, rigidity and tremor; generally reversible.
**Delayed neuropathy at 1–3 weeks.** Distal, sensory then motor, ascending (PEST-07).
mimic: Delayed cholinergic phase vs intermediate syndrome
Returning secretions and miosis need atropine; pure weakness with a dry chest does not.
traps: “Everything happens in the first 24 hours”
Most syndromes begin after 24 hours — observe at least four days, follow up for weeks.
decode: Reappearance of secretions at 44 hours after a fat-soluble OP [pattern]
Delayed-onset cholinergic phase — atropine again.
Dystonia 10 days later [pattern]
Extrapyramidal syndrome.
PEST-08.punch: The poisoning unfolds for three weeks, and the order is mechanistic: continuing absorption, then the junction, then the brain, then the axon — so observation is measured in days and follow-up in weeks.

PEST-09.sub: Toxicology → Pesticides → Diagnosis: cholinesterases and the atropine challenge
PEST-09.intro: The diagnosis is clinical, but two blood enzymes answer different questions. One is the synapse’s own enzyme and tracks how poisoned the patient is; the other is a liver protein that merely proves exposure. Where neither assay is available, a small dose of atropine can serve as a test.
why: **RBC cholinesterase is true (acetyl) cholinesterase: it mirrors the synaptic enzyme and correlates with severity.** Mild 20–50% of normal, moderate 10–20%, severe under 10% — with coma, flaccid paralysis, pulmonary oedema and pinpoint pupils. Red cells cannot resynthesise it, so recovery is about 1% a day.

**Plasma cholinesterase is pseudo (butyryl) cholinesterase, made in the liver: a simple marker of exposure with no correlation with severity.** It is a sensitive screen, but its baseline varies widely and falls in liver disease, pregnancy and malnutrition; its practical use is a warning that suxamethonium will be prolonged (PEST-12).

**Atropine challenge: a rise in heart rate of more than 20–25/min with flushing after a small dose means no significant cholinergic poisoning.** A poisoned patient’s receptors are swamped with acetylcholine, so a small competitive dose changes little.
traps: “Plasma cholinesterase correlates with severity”
It does not — the RBC enzyme does.
“Wait for the assay before giving atropine”
Treatment is clinical and immediate; the assay confirms.
decode: RBC AChE 8% of normal with coma and flaccid paralysis: severity? [pattern]
Severe (<10%).
Heart rate rises 30/min after 1 mg atropine [pattern]
No significant cholinergic poisoning.
PEST-09.punch: The red cell enzyme is the synapse in a tube and grades severity; plasma cholinesterase only says the patient met the poison — and a patient who shrugs off a test dose of atropine is the one who needs it.

PEST-10.intro: Atropine is a competitive muscarinic antagonist, so it must outnumber the acetylcholine piling up in the synapse — the dose is whatever it takes. What it is competing for is the airway: secretions and bronchospasm kill in the first hours. So the dose is escalated fast and judged by the chest, not by the pupils or the pulse.
why: **2–5 mg IV, doubling every 5 minutes until atropinised.** Fixed small doses lose the race against a flooded synapse, so the dose is doubled — 2, 4, 8, 16 mg — until the end-points are met; giving too little is the commoner error. Atropine is the life-saving first drug; with an oxime alongside in moderate to severe poisoning, it is the initial management (TOXBASE: immediate bolus then infusion).

**End-points: a clear chest with no wheeze or secretions, heart rate above 80, systolic pressure above 80, dry axillae, and pupils no longer pinpoint.** Drying of respiratory secretions is the one that matters, because bronchorrhoea is the lethal effect. The heart-rate target is only above 80 — tachycardia over 100 is not the goal; mydriasis and hypertension are not end-points, and pupils are the least reliable sign.
**Maintenance by infusion of 10–20% of the total loading dose per hour.** Atropine lasts a few hours while the organophosphate persists for days, so stopping after loading lets the patient relapse.
**If atropine toxicity occurs, stop, then restart at 70–80% of the previous rate.** Over-atropinisation gives agitation, delirium, hyperthermia, ileus, urinary retention and tachyarrhythmia.
**It does not treat the nicotinic effects: weakness and paralysis.** There are no muscarinic receptors at the neuromuscular junction; those need an oxime and often a ventilator (PEST-11, PEST-05).
mimic: Atropine toxicity vs continuing poisoning
Both give a confused, tachycardic patient; atropine excess has a dry chest, absent bowel sounds and a full bladder, continuing poisoning a wet, wheezy chest.
traps: “Atropinisation means heart rate >100 or dilated pupils”
The end-point is a dry chest and axillae with clear lungs; HR >80 is enough. Only 63% chose this.
“Gastric lavage in all cases, haemodialysis or steroids”
None is initial management; immediate atropine bolus then infusion is.
“Tachycardia is a reason to withhold atropine”
A wet chest still needs atropine.
decode: What guides adequate atropinisation during titration? [DocT]
Dry axilla and chest, clear lungs.
Endpoint of continuous IV atropine [DocT]
Drying of respiratory secretions.
TOXBASE initial management of moderate OP poisoning [DocT]
Immediate atropine bolus followed by infusion.
Farmer with SLUDGE and miosis: initial step [DocT]
Atropine and pralidoxime together.
PEST-10.punch: Atropine is titrated against the airway and nothing else: double the dose until the chest is clear and the axillae dry, keep an infusion going because the poison outlasts the drug, and accept that weakness is not its business.

PEST-11.intro: Atropine blocks the receptor; an oxime takes the phosphate off the enzyme and gives the synapse its acetylcholinesterase back. That is the only way the nicotinic effects — fasciculation, weakness, respiratory muscle failure — can be treated. It works only while the bond is still rescuable, so it is started at once and given as an infusion.
why: **Pralidoxime, obidoxime, trimedoxime.** All quaternary oximes; pralidoxime is the one available in India.

**They bind the anionic site and pull the phosphate off the esteratic site, reactivating cholinesterase before ageing; they also slow further ageing.** The reactivated enzyme clears acetylcholine again. Pralidoxime does not block receptors, enhance renal excretion of the poison or stop it binding red cells — it reactivates the enzyme.

**Pralidoxime 1–2 g over 30 minutes, repeated in 1 hour if weakness persists, or given as an infusion.** WHO dosing: 30 mg/kg (about 2 g) over 30 minutes, then 8 mg/kg/h (about 500 mg/h) until atropine is no longer needed. An infusion holds the plasma level (above about 4 mg/L) needed to outpace re-inhibition.
**Not recommended in carbamate poisoning, but do not withhold it when the agent is unknown.** Carbamylated enzyme recovers on its own; an unidentified bottle may be an organophosphate.

**Useless once the enzyme has aged; no CNS effect; rapid injection causes laryngospasm, hypertension and vomiting.** Being permanently charged, pralidoxime scarcely enters the brain; it is infused over 30 minutes.
mimic: Atropine vs pralidoxime
Atropine blocks muscarinic receptors and treats secretions; pralidoxime restores the enzyme and treats nicotinic weakness. Organophosphates, sarin included, get both.
traps: “After atropine, persisting bronchorrhoea, miosis or bradycardia indicates pralidoxime”
Those are muscarinic — more atropine. Fasciculation (nicotinic) is the indication [NEET 2025].
“Pralidoxime instead of atropine if secretions are heavy”
It has no muscarinic action.
“Trial evidence proves oximes work”
It does not: a placebo-controlled trial of the WHO regimen showed no clinical benefit and the Cochrane review finds the evidence insufficient. They are still given early, with atropine.
decode: Action of pralidoxime [DocT ×2]
Reactivates acetylcholinesterase by removing the organophosphate.
Pralidoxime dosing in severe OP poisoning [DocT]
2 g IV over 30 min, then 500 mg/h infusion.
After atropine, finding indicating pralidoxime [NEET 2025]
Muscle fasciculations.
Cholinergic crisis after suicide attempt / severe sarin: effective combination [Marrow / DocT GT]
Atropine and pralidoxime.
PEST-11.punch: An oxime is the only drug that gives the enzyme back, so it is the only treatment for nicotinic weakness — started early, infused rather than pushed, and worthless once the bond has aged.
fix: Pralidoxime works if given in time

The evidence is insufficient either way (Cochrane): the Sri Lankan placebo-controlled trial of the WHO regimen showed no benefit, a small Indian trial of 1 g/h for 48 h showed fewer deaths. WHO regimen: 30 mg/kg (~2 g) over 30 min, then 8 mg/kg/h.

PEST-12.intro: Beyond atropine and an oxime, management is airway, decontamination and avoiding harm. Two details are specific: the relaxant used for intubation is cleared by the enzyme the poison has inhibited, and the poison is still on the skin and in the vomit — absorbed by the patient and by the staff.
why: **Avoid succinylcholine: it is metabolised by plasma cholinesterase, so paralysis is prolonged.** With the plasma enzyme inhibited a standard dose can paralyse for hours. Use rocuronium.

**Remove clothes and wash the skin; activated charcoal 1 g/kg within 1 hour; no forced emesis.** Organophosphates are absorbed through skin and evaporate from soaked clothing and vomit, so staff need full protective gear against both dermal and inhaled exposure — gloves, gown, eye protection and a ventilated space. Induced emesis risks aspiration in a patient who may convulse.

**Glycopyrrolate does not cross the blood–brain barrier: added to atropine it caused far less confusion and hallucination (30% versus 90%) and less tachyarrhythmia, with the same outcome. Dose 7.5 mg in 200 mL, infused until the mucous membranes are dry.** It dries secretions without central delirium, but cannot replace atropine for central effects.

**Fresh frozen plasma is harmful; haemodialysis and bicarbonate have no role; magnesium has no scientific data, and clonidine and vitamin E rest on animal studies only.** FFP raised plasma cholinesterase in the one randomised pilot but did not improve deaths or ventilator days — no benefit rather than proven harm. Organophosphates are lipophilic with a large volume of distribution, so dialysis removes nothing useful. Magnesium is better described as unproven: small trials hint at benefit but are insufficient to recommend it.
mimic: Glycopyrrolate vs atropine
Glycopyrrolate dries without delirium but has no central action; atropine remains the drug titrated to the chest (PEST-10).
traps: “Gloves are enough” / “decontamination is only for the patient”
Vomit and clothing release the agent; full dermal and inhalational protection is needed.
“Give fresh frozen plasma to replace cholinesterase”
No improvement in survival; not a treatment.
“Dialyse the organophosphate”
Large volume of distribution — dialysis removes nothing useful.
decode: Cholinergic patient vomiting, chemical smell: staff precaution [Marrow]
Full protective gear — dermal and inhalational.
Intubating drug to avoid [pattern]
Succinylcholine — prolonged block.
PEST-12.punch: The extras are mostly about not adding harm: no succinylcholine, no forced emesis, no dialysis, never FFP — while the things that do work are washing the patient, protecting the team and keeping the chest dry.
fix: FFP: harmful
The only randomised pilot (Vellore 2010) showed no benefit, not proven harm: FFP is not recommended. For the exam’s ‘which is harmful’ it is still the intended answer.
Magnesium: no scientific data
There are four small randomised trials and cohorts with a possible mortality benefit (Brvar 2018), but the evidence is still insufficient to recommend it.

PEST-13.intro: These eight statements are the deck’s key discriminations, and each turns on a mechanism met earlier: which alkyl group ages faster, which enzyme is the synapse’s own, which receptor each antidote reaches, and which muscles fail when.
why: **False — dimethyl compounds age in about 3 hours, diethyl in about 33.** The smaller methyl group is shed more readily (PEST-03).
**False — the RBC (true) enzyme correlates with severity.** Under 10% of normal is severe, 10–20% moderate, 20–50% mild; plasma butyrylcholinesterase shows exposure only (PEST-09).
**False — the intermediate syndrome affects neck flexors and proximal muscles first.** Distal, ascending weakness at 1–3 weeks is the delayed neuropathy (PEST-05, PEST-07).
**False — delayed neuropathy is independent of acute severity.** It follows inhibition of neuropathy target esterase (PEST-07).
**False — fasciculation is nicotinic, and atropine is purely antimuscarinic.** Only an oxime addresses it (PEST-10, PEST-11).
**False — oximes are not recommended in carbamate poisoning.** Carbamylated enzyme hydrolyses spontaneously; they are still given when the agent is unknown (PEST-11).
**True — atropinisation is judged by a dry chest.** Clear lungs and dry axillae are the end-point (PEST-10).
**False — tachycardia does not exclude organophosphate poisoning.** Ganglionic stimulation, hypoxia and bronchospasm raise the rate (PEST-04).
mimic: Severe acute poisoning vs intermediate syndrome
Coma, flaccid paralysis, pulmonary oedema and pinpoint pupils on arrival is severe cholinergic poisoning; the intermediate syndrome comes later, in a conscious patient after the crisis.
traps: “Flaccid paralysis means intermediate syndrome”
On presentation, with coma and RBC AChE <10%, it is severe cholinergic poisoning.
“Atropine covers the whole syndrome”
It covers only the muscarinic part.
decode: Flaccid paralysis, coma, pulmonary oedema, pinpoint pupils, RBC AChE 8%: classify [DocT GT]
Severe cholinergic poisoning.
Statements about ageing or antidotes [pattern]
Which alkyl group (dimethyl is fast); which receptor the drug reaches.
PEST-13.punch: Every statement here comes back to three questions: which alkyl group is on the phosphorus, which enzyme is being measured, and which receptor the antidote can actually reach.

PEST-14.intro: A rodenticide has to kill a rat that eats only a little bait, so many are poisons of the cell’s basic machinery. Human toxicity depends on how potent the chemical is and how much is in the bait. In India three groups dominate — yellow phosphorus paste, metal phosphide tablets and the long-acting anticoagulants — and they sit in very different places on this scale.
why: **Highly toxic: yellow phosphorus, metal phosphides, strychnine, arsenic, sodium monofluoroacetate.** Each attacks something every cell needs: yellow phosphorus causes fatty degeneration of the liver (PEST-15); phosphine blocks cytochrome c oxidase (PEST-18); monofluoroacetate becomes fluorocitrate and blocks aconitase in the citric acid cycle; strychnine blocks inhibitory glycine receptors; arsenic binds enzyme thiol groups. Small amounts kill, and most have no antidote.

**Moderately toxic: alpha-naphthyl thiourea (ANTU), cholecalciferol.** ANTU raises pulmonary capillary permeability, causing pulmonary oedema and effusion. Cholecalciferol causes hypercalcaemia over days.

**Less toxic: superwarfarins, red squill, bromethalin.** Superwarfarin baits contain very little drug, so an accidental mouthful rarely matters — a deliberate large ingestion still causes weeks of coagulopathy (PEST-17). Red squill is a cardiac glycoside but a strong emetic, and humans, unlike rats, vomit it up.
mimic: Strychnine vs tetanus
Both give spasms with a clear sensorium; strychnine starts within an hour and muscles relax fully between spasms, tetanus starts days after a wound with persisting rigidity.
traps: “Superwarfarins are less toxic, so a large ingestion can be sent home”
‘Less toxic’ refers to the dilute bait; many packets cause coagulopathy for weeks to months.
decode: Ratol paste vs Celphos tablet vs rat-poison cake [pattern]
Yellow phosphorus (liver, day 3); aluminium phosphide (shock, hours); superwarfarin (bleeding, days).
PEST-14.punch: The most toxic rodenticides poison what every cell needs — the mitochondria, the citric acid cycle, inhibitory synapses — while the least toxic are either dilute in the bait or make the patient vomit.

PEST-15.sub: Toxicology → Rodenticides → Yellow phosphorus vs metal phosphide
PEST-15.intro: Both poisons contain phosphorus and both smell of garlic, but they kill on different clocks. Yellow phosphorus poisons the liver cell itself, so the patient may look well for a day before liver failure. A metal phosphide releases phosphine, which switches off cellular respiration everywhere, so the circulation fails within hours.
why: **Form: yellow phosphorus as a paste (Ratol); metal phosphide as tablets (Celphos) or zinc phosphide powder.** A 3 g Celphos tablet releases about 1 g of phosphine on contact with moisture — far more than a lethal dose.

**Mechanism: yellow phosphorus is a protoplasmic toxin causing fatty degeneration of liver, kidney and brain; phosphide releases phosphine with acid or water, which blocks mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation.** Phosphorus stops the hepatocyte exporting fat, so it accumulates and the cell dies. Phosphine inhibits cytochrome c oxidase, so cells with the highest demand — myocardium and vascular smooth muscle — fail first.

**Course: yellow phosphorus mild on day 1, transaminitis on day 2, liver failure on day 3; phosphide shock and multi-organ failure within 30 minutes.** The phosphorus delay is the time liver cells take to die, so an early ‘well’ patient must be admitted; phosphine acts as soon as it forms.
**Clue: luminescent faeces and garlic odour with yellow phosphorus; garlic odour with phosphide.** Elemental phosphorus glows as it oxidises in air.
**Death: yellow phosphorus by liver failure; phosphide by circulatory failure.** Phosphine causes myocardial depression, arrhythmias and vasodilatation together, so the shock is refractory (PEST-18).
**Antidote: none for either.** Decontamination and support; for yellow phosphorus, liver support up to transplantation (PEST-16).
mimic: Yellow phosphorus vs paracetamol
Both look mild at first and fail the liver around day 3; paracetamol has NAC and a nomogram, phosphorus has neither.
traps: “The Ratol patient is well on day 1, so discharge”
Transaminases rise on day 2 and failure comes on day 3.
“Luminescent faeces suggest phosphide”
It is yellow phosphorus — the elemental form glows.
decode: Garlic odour, glowing stool, jaundice on day 3 [pattern]
Yellow phosphorus.
Garlic odour, BP 70/40 two hours after a tablet [pattern]
Aluminium phosphide.
PEST-15.punch: Same element, two clocks: yellow phosphorus slowly poisons the liver cell and kills on day 3, while phosphine shuts down mitochondria everywhere and kills the circulation within hours.
fix: Shock and multi-organ failure within 30 minutes
Vomiting starts within minutes, but shock usually develops over 1–6 hours and most deaths come within 24 hours.

PEST-16.intro: There is no antidote to yellow phosphorus, so treatment follows the course: limit absorption early, support the failing liver and its clotting factors, and replace the liver if it does not recover.
why: **Lavage with potassium permanganate, which oxidises phosphorus; avoid oily or fatty food, which increases absorption.** Permanganate converts elemental phosphorus to less absorbable phosphates; phosphorus dissolves in fat, so oil carries it across the gut wall.

**Vitamin K, FFP or prothrombin complex for bleeding, electrolytes, N-acetylcysteine.** The damaged liver cannot make clotting factors, so they are replaced when the patient bleeds. NAC is supportive, as in other non-paracetamol liver failure — not an antidote.

**Plasma exchange in liver failure lowered INR and transaminases significantly; bilirubin was unchanged.** Exchange removes toxin and replaces clotting factors with donor plasma, so the INR falls; much bilirubin sits in the tissues, so it barely moves. It buys time for regeneration or transplant.
**Liver transplant as the last resort.** When the liver fails and does not recover, transplant is the only definitive treatment.
traps: “Give vegetable oil to bind the phosphorus”
Phosphorus dissolves in fat, so oils and fatty food increase absorption.
decode: Lavage fluid for yellow phosphorus [pattern]
Potassium permanganate.
Ratol poisoning, rising INR on day 3: bridge to recovery [pattern]
Plasma exchange.
PEST-16.punch: Without an antidote, yellow phosphorus is treated by its timeline: oxidise and avoid fat early, replace clotting factors as the liver fails, exchange plasma to buy time, and transplant if the liver does not come back.
fix: WATCH: vegetable oil lavage
Digestible oils increase phosphorus absorption; older texts used liquid paraffin (not absorbed). Gastric lavage of any kind is not routine now.

PEST-17.intro: The second-generation ‘superwarfarins’ were made after rats became resistant to warfarin: they bind the same enzyme far more tightly and stay in the liver for weeks. In a human that means a coagulopathy that starts late and lasts long.
why: **Brodifacoum, bromadiolone, difenacoum, chlorophacinone.** All are fat-soluble and concentrate in the liver, giving half-lives of weeks.

**Inhibit vitamin K epoxide reductase, so no active factors II, VII, IX and X are made.** Vitamin K must be recycled by this reductase after each use; blocked, the liver releases factors that cannot work.

**Bleeding begins at 24–48 hours, once the existing factors fall below 30%.** The drug stops new factors being made but leaves circulating ones, so nothing happens until they run out; factor VII goes first, so the INR rises first.
**Confirmation by 4-hydroxycoumarin level on mass spectrometry.** The level confirms the agent and, repeated, shows when it has cleared.

**Vitamin K1 in high doses for weeks to months; FFP or prothrombin complex for active bleeding.** High-dose vitamin K1 uses an alternative pathway the poison does not block; the drug lasts weeks, so treatment does too, guided by the INR. Vitamin K takes hours, so a bleeding patient also needs factors replaced.
mimic: Superwarfarin vs warfarin overdose vs liver failure
Warfarin wears off in days, a superwarfarin lasts weeks to months; liver failure also lowers factor V and fibrinogen, which vitamin K antagonism spares.
traps: “Normal INR on the day of ingestion — safe to discharge”
The existing factors have not yet run out; repeat the INR at 48 hours.
“A single dose of vitamin K reverses it”
High doses are needed for weeks to months.
decode: Unexplained high INR with bleeding, no warfarin, normal liver; INR recurs when vitamin K stops [pattern]
Superwarfarin ingestion — high-dose vitamin K1 for weeks.
PEST-17.punch: Superwarfarins stop new clotting factors being made but leave the old ones, so the INR is normal until they run out at 24–48 hours — and because the drug stays in the liver for weeks, so must the vitamin K.
fix: A 4-hydroxycoumarin level covers the superwarfarins
Chlorophacinone is an indandione, not a 4-hydroxycoumarin. The INR rises at 24–48 h, but bleeding may only appear days later.

PEST-18.intro: Aluminium phosphide is a cheap grain fumigant, freely available in rural North India and one of the commonest suicidal poisons there. Each tablet releases phosphine in the moist, acid stomach. Phosphine stops the last step of energy production, so the heart and vessels fail first.
why: **26% of pesticide poisonings in a North Indian series (PGI Chandigarh).** Common where grain is stored, with high mortality.
**Phosphine, which inhibits cytochrome c oxidase.** Complex IV, the last enzyme of the respiratory chain: ATP production collapses, free radicals form and lactate rises.

**Vomiting, refractory shock, myocarditis and arrhythmias, severe metabolic acidosis, within minutes to hours.** The shock combines a failing myocardium with vasodilatation, so fluids and vasopressors work poorly; the acidosis is lactic.

**Supportive only; magnesium sulphate is used but unproven.** No antidote: early ventilation, careful fluids, vasopressors and inotropes; VA-ECMO can carry the heart through the first 24–48 hours. Magnesium trials conflict.
mimic: Aluminium phosphide vs organophosphate
Both are garlic-smelling pesticides; the organophosphate patient has a cholinergic toxidrome, the phosphide patient shock and acidosis without one.
traps: “Shock is hypovolaemic, so give large volumes of fluid”
The heart is failing; large volumes worsen pulmonary oedema. Guide fluids by echo and use inotropes.
decode: Grain-storage tablet, refractory shock, severe acidosis: agent, toxin, target [pattern]
Aluminium phosphide; phosphine; cytochrome c oxidase — supportive care.
PEST-18.punch: Phosphine blocks the last step of the respiratory chain, so the heart and vessels fail first and the shock resists treatment — and with no antidote, survival depends on supporting the circulation through the first day.

PEST-19.intro: Paraquat is a contact herbicide that destroys plant tissue by generating free radicals. Swallowed, it is one of the deadliest poisons in agricultural Asia: a small volume of concentrate kills, and there is no antidote.
why: **Bipyridyl herbicide.** Two linked pyridine rings accept and give away electrons easily — the basis of its toxicity (PEST-20). Diquat is the other member.
**10–20 mL of the 20% concentrate.** That is 2–4 g, about 30–60 mg/kg in an adult (PEST-21): a single mouthful can be fatal.
**Ingestion is dangerous; inhalation and skin contact are not life-threatening.** Spray droplets are too large to reach the alveoli and intact skin absorbs little.
**Case fatality up to 70%.** Death is quick from multi-organ failure after a large dose, or slow from pulmonary fibrosis after a moderate one.
mimic: Paraquat vs diquat
Diquat spares the lung (no active alveolar uptake) and injures kidney and brain instead.
traps: “The patient only swallowed a mouthful, so it is minor”
10–20 mL of the concentrate is a lethal dose.
decode: Weedkiller ingestion, mouth ulcers, breathlessness at 1–2 weeks [pattern]
Paraquat.
PEST-19.punch: Paraquat is lethal only when swallowed, but then a single mouthful of the 20% concentrate can kill — and there is nothing to reverse it.
fix: Skin contact is not life-threatening
True for intact skin and diluted spray; fatal poisoning has been reported after prolonged contact of the concentrate with damaged skin.

PEST-20.intro: Paraquat is not consumed when it does harm: it shuttles electrons to oxygen again and again, making free radicals every time. The organs it injures most are those that take it up actively, and in the lung that uptake meets the highest oxygen tension in the body.
why: **Redox cycling generates reactive oxygen species, with mitochondrial failure.** NADPH-dependent enzymes reduce paraquat to a radical, which hands its electron to oxygen as superoxide and returns ready to cycle again — damaging membranes and draining NADPH.

**Active uptake by alveolar cells through the polyamine uptake system, causing alveolitis and then pulmonary fibrosis.** Paraquat resembles natural polyamines, so alveolar cells pump it in and concentrate it; with abundant oxygen the cycle runs fastest. Alveolitis comes first, fibrosis over one to three weeks.
**Accumulation in proximal tubular cells, causing tubular necrosis.** The kidney is the only route of elimination; as it fails, more paraquat reaches the lung.
**Oxygen is the substrate for free-radical formation.** Extra oxygen accelerates the injury, so it is withheld unless the patient is hypoxic.
traps: “Give high-flow oxygen as in every poisoning”
Oxygen feeds the redox cycle; give it only for hypoxia.
decode: Why is oxygen withheld in paraquat poisoning? [pattern]
Oxygen is the substrate for the redox cycle that forms free radicals.
Transport concentrating paraquat in the lung [pattern]
The polyamine uptake system of alveolar cells.
PEST-20.punch: Paraquat recycles itself, handing electrons to oxygen to make free radicals; the lung pumps it in and is full of oxygen, so the lung fibroses — and giving more oxygen only feeds the cycle.

PEST-21.intro: Because the redox cycle runs as long as paraquat is present, outcome is set mainly by the dose swallowed — which predicts not just whether the patient dies but how.
why: **Mild: below 20 mg/kg — GI symptoms only, full recovery.** Under about 7 mL of the concentrate; too little reaches the lung to start fibrosis.
**Moderate to severe: 20–40 mg/kg — renal and hepatic failure, then pulmonary fibrosis; death in 2–3 weeks.** The patient may seem to improve, then becomes steadily more hypoxic as the lung fibroses.
**Fulminant: above 40 mg/kg — multi-organ failure and shock; death in 1–4 days.** Heart, liver, kidneys and adrenals fail together, before fibrosis has time to develop.
traps: “Early recovery from the GI phase means survival”
In the 20–40 mg/kg group, fibrosis progresses over the following weeks.
decode: Paraquat 30 mg/kg, improving on day 3 [pattern]
Moderate–severe: expect progressive fibrosis, death in 2–3 weeks.
PEST-21.punch: Paraquat severity follows the dose: under 20 mg/kg the gut recovers, 20–40 mg/kg the lung fibroses over weeks, and above 40 mg/kg the whole body fails in days.

PEST-22.intro: With no antidote, the useful questions are ‘was it paraquat?’ and ‘will this patient survive?’. A bedside urine test answers the first; the plasma level read against time since ingestion answers the second.
why: **Sodium dithionite in alkali added to urine gives a blue colour; best within 6 hours.** Dithionite reduces paraquat to its blue radical; most is excreted early, so a late sample can be falsely negative.

**Severity Index of Paraquat Poisoning (SIPP) = plasma level (mg/L) × hours since ingestion; below 10, survival is likely.** A given level means more the later it is taken, because it should be falling; multiplying by time corrects for this.
**Other poor signs: lactate above 4, renal failure, ARDS.** Lactate means cellular respiration is failing; renal failure shuts the only exit; early ARDS signals a large lung dose.
mimic: Paraquat vs diquat in the dithionite test
Paraquat turns blue; diquat gives green.
traps: “A plasma level alone predicts outcome”
It must be read against the time since ingestion.
decode: Urine turns blue with sodium dithionite [pattern]
Paraquat.
Plasma level × hours since ingestion [pattern]
SIPP; below 10, survival likely.
PEST-22.punch: Dithionite turns paraquat blue by the same reduction that makes it toxic, and prognosis comes from the plasma level read against time — because a level that should have fallen but has not means death.

PEST-23.intro: Paraquat moves from plasma into lung and kidney within hours, and once there no treatment pulls it out. So treatment is binding what remains in the gut, keeping the kidneys excreting, and not feeding the injury with oxygen.
why: **Avoid oxygen unless hypoxic; hydration; no forced emesis (caustic); wash skin and eyes; Fuller’s earth or activated charcoal early.** Oxygen feeds the redox cycle (PEST-20); fluids keep the only exit open; emesis brings the corrosive back over the oesophagus; adsorbents work only before absorption.

**Experimental: immunosuppression (dexamethasone, cyclophosphamide), N-acetylcysteine, vitamins C and E, edaravone — none proven.** Immunosuppression aims at the alveolitis, the antioxidants at the radicals; the largest steroid–cyclophosphamide trial showed no significant survival benefit.

**Haemofiltration: a meta-analysis of 3 trials showed no reduction in mortality (risk ratio 0.94).** It removes only plasma paraquat; within hours most has moved into the lung and kidney, beyond reach.
**False — luminescent faeces suggest yellow phosphorus.** Elemental phosphorus glows as it oxidises (PEST-15).
**False — superwarfarin bleeding starts at 24–48 hours.** The circulating factors must be used up first (PEST-17).
mimic: Oxygen in paraquat vs in carbon monoxide
In CO, 100% oxygen is the treatment (TOX-13); in paraquat it feeds the injury.
traps: “Haemoperfusion or haemofiltration removes paraquat from the lung”
Only plasma paraquat is removed; tissue uptake happens within hours.
decode: Best early step in paraquat ingestion [pattern]
Fuller’s earth or activated charcoal, fluids, no oxygen unless hypoxic.
PEST-23.punch: Paraquat leaves the plasma for the lung within hours and cannot be pulled back, so care is early binding, fluids and withholding oxygen — and when the dose is lethal, honest palliative care.

REC-01.sub: Toxicology → Cannabis & Opioids → Substance use in India
REC-01.intro: The figures come from the 2019 national survey of substance use in India (NDDTC, AIIMS), which counted current users aged 10–75. Alcohol far outnumbers everything else, opioid use is well above the world rate, and children have a pattern of their own.
why: **Alcohol, 14.6%.** About one in seven Indians aged 10–75 is a current drinker — which is why alcohol withdrawal and alcohol-related liver disease are the commonest substance problems on the ward.

**Cannabis 2.8%, then opioids 2.1%.** Cannabis is cheap and culturally familiar (bhang), so it comes second. Opioids come third, but at 2.1% Indian use is about three times the global figure (0.7%), and heroin has overtaken opium as the commonest opioid.

**Inhalants.** Glue, whitener and solvent sprays are cheap, legal and easy to hide. The survey’s point is that inhalants are the one class used more by children and adolescents than by adults — not that they are children’s commonest substance overall.
traps: “Cannabis is the commonest substance used in India”
Alcohol is far ahead at 14.6%; cannabis is second at 2.8%.
“Opioid use in India is below the world average”
It is about three times the global figure — 2.1% vs 0.7%.
decode: Commonest substance of abuse in India (national survey) [pattern]
Alcohol.
Substance used more by children than by adults [pattern]
Inhalants.
REC-01.punch: Alcohol dominates Indian substance use, cannabis and opioids follow — with opioid use three times the world rate — and inhalants are the drug of children.
fix: In children: inhalants
Inhalants are the only class used more by children than by adults (about 1.17% vs 0.58%, 2019 national survey); they are not the commonest substance in children.

REC-02.intro: Cannabis acts on the body’s own endocannabinoid receptors, which fine-tune neurotransmitter release. They sit mainly in the brain and hardly at all in the brainstem respiratory centres, so plain cannabis disturbs the mind but spares breathing, and its treatment is supportive. A seizing, hyperthermic ‘cannabis’ user has usually taken a synthetic cannabinoid.
why: **Delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol.** THC is the main psychoactive cannabinoid. It is highly lipid-soluble, stored in fat and released slowly, which is why a chronic user stays urine-positive for weeks (TOX-02).

**CB1: CNS (basal ganglia, cerebellum, hypothalamus). CB2: periphery (spleen, immune cells).** CB1 receptors on presynaptic terminals dampen transmitter release, and their distribution matches the effects — incoordination (basal ganglia, cerebellum), appetite (hypothalamus), memory (hippocampus). CB1 is scarce in the brainstem, so cannabis alone does not stop breathing. CB2 modulates inflammation.

**Bhang (crushed leaves), ganja and charas (smoked), hashish (resin of flowering tops).** Bhang is drunk or eaten, so it acts slowly and for longer; resins are concentrated and carry more THC per gram.

**Supportive; a short-acting benzodiazepine for agitation; exclude other drugs.** There is no antidote. Panic, psychosis and tachycardia settle with calm and a benzodiazepine. Coma or seizures point to a co-ingestant or a synthetic cannabinoid — which is also treated first with benzodiazepines, because they lower the central drive that produces the agitation, heat and seizures.
mimic: Cannabis vs synthetic cannabinoids (spice, K2)
Synthetic cannabinoids are full CB1 agonists: a sympathomimetic picture with seizures, agitated delirium, hyperthermia and AKI — and the urine drug screen is negative.
traps: “CB1 receptors are mainly peripheral”
CB1 is the central receptor; CB2 is on immune cells (REC-14a).
“A negative urine screen excludes cannabinoid toxicity”
Synthetic cannabinoids are not detected by the standard immunoassay.
“Haloperidol, a beta-blocker or phentolamine first for synthetic-cannabinoid agitation and hyperthermia”
Benzodiazepines first: haloperidol lowers the seizure threshold and impairs heat loss, and the beta-blocker or vasodilator treats a number, not the drive.
decode: Synthetic cannabinoid overdose with severe agitation and hyperthermia — best initial treatment [DocT]
Benzodiazepines.
Seizure, sympathomimetic picture, negative urine screen, says he smoked ‘cannabis’ [Marrow]
Synthetic cannabinoid.
REC-02.punch: THC acts on central CB1 receptors that are scarce in the brainstem, so cannabis disturbs the mind but spares breathing — care is supportive, and seizures with a negative screen mean a synthetic cannabinoid, treated first with benzodiazepines.

REC-03.sub: Toxicology → Cannabis & Opioids → Opioid overdose and naloxone
REC-03.intro: Opioids stimulate μ receptors in the brainstem, which blunts the response to carbon dioxide; breathing slows, then stops, and hypoxia is what kills. Naloxone is a competitive μ antagonist that displaces the opioid within minutes — it, not flumazenil, charcoal or a urine screen, is the first step. But naloxone leaves the receptor sooner than most opioids, so a patient who wakes can stop breathing again.
why: **Coma, pinpoint pupils, respiratory depression.** μ stimulation depresses the reticular activating system (coma) and the respiratory centre, and releases the Edinger–Westphal nucleus, so the pupils constrict (TOX-04); heart rate and blood pressure often fall too. Small pupils with a respiratory rate below about 10 point to an opioid — including codeine derivatives such as dihydrocodeine — rather than a benzodiazepine, which leaves breathing near normal (REC-09).

**3,6-diacetylmorphine; 2–3 times as potent as morphine.** The two acetyl groups make heroin far more lipid-soluble, so it enters the brain fast before being deacetylated to 6-monoacetylmorphine and morphine, which act on the receptor.

**0.2–0.4 mg IV or IM, repeated to a maximum of 2 mg (0.04 mg steps in the dependent).** The aim is breathing (RR about 12 or more), not full wakefulness. In an opioid-dependent patient a large dose strips every receptor at once and causes abrupt withdrawal — agitation, vomiting and even seizures — so small steps are used.

**40–80 minutes (your notes also print 30–120): shorter than most opioids, so toxicity recurs.** In round numbers, about an hour. Morphine, methadone and sustained-release preparations outlast a naloxone bolus, so a patient who responds still needs continued monitoring — prolonged with long-acting or sustained-release drugs — not discharge on waking.

**Two-thirds of the effective reversal dose per hour.** The dose that woke the patient is known to work; two-thirds of it each hour as an infusion keeps receptor occupancy roughly steady. It is adjusted to breathing and to signs of withdrawal.
mimic: Opioid vs clonidine coma
Both give miosis, coma and bradycardia, but clonidine responds poorly to naloxone (TOX-04) — pinpoint pupils alone do not confirm an opioid.
Pulmonary oedema after naloxone vs heroin lung injury

Abrupt reversal causes a sympathetic (catecholamine) surge, and the waking patient gasps against a closed glottis: neurogenic, non-cardiogenic oedema — not heroin alveolar toxicity or myocardial depression. One more reason to titrate.
traps: “Naloxone lasts 6–12 hours, so one dose is enough”
It lasts about an hour (40–80 minutes), less than most opioids; re-sedation is the rule with long-acting drugs (REC-14b).
“Seizures after naloxone in a heroin user are hypoxic”
They are precipitated withdrawal — the dose stripped the receptors too fast; titrate from 0.04 mg in the dependent.
“Still drowsy after naloxone though breathing is restored — tolerance or delayed opioid toxicity”

Naloxone restores breathing, not necessarily consciousness; a co-ingested sedative (benzodiazepine, alcohol, gabapentinoid) is the usual answer, then hypoglycaemia, head injury or hypoxic brain injury.
“Coma, small pupils, RR 8, hypotension, low tone — diazepam”
Benzodiazepines rarely depress breathing this much on their own; small pupils with a slow rate mean an opioid (dihydrocodeine).
decode: Unconscious, pinpoint pupils, RR 6 — next step (flumazenil, intubation and CT offered) [DocT; NEET 2025]
Naloxone.
RR improves after naloxone but remains drowsy [DocT]
Co-ingested sedative-hypnotic.
Heroin user develops pulmonary oedema or seizures after the antidote [DocT]
Sympathetic surge (neurogenic oedema); precipitated withdrawal.
How long does naloxone act? [DocT]
About 60 minutes — keep monitoring, especially with sustained-release opioids.
REC-03.punch: Naloxone pushes the opioid off the μ receptor, but it leaves first — so it is titrated to breathing rather than wakefulness, and followed by an infusion or observation when the opioid will outlast it.
fix: Naloxone to a maximum of 2 mg
2 mg is not a ceiling: up to about 10 mg is given before opioid toxicity is ruled out (more often needed with fentanyl analogues).

REC-04.intro: A body packer swallows many tightly wrapped packets of heroin or cocaine to smuggle them. Each packet holds many times a lethal dose. The packer is well while the wrapping holds; if one leaks, the gut absorbs a massive dose at once — and which drug is inside decides whether there is an antidote.
why: **Massive toxicity from rupture of swallowed drug packets (heroin or cocaine).** Acid, peristalsis and time can split a packet, and the gut absorbs freely, so one rupture gives an overdose far larger than street use. A packer who suddenly develops hypotension, VT or confusion has a ruptured packet until proved otherwise. An intact packet can still obstruct the bowel.
**Packets may be radio-opaque.** They often show as regular oval shapes on a plain film (TOX-08), but X-ray misses some; CT is more sensitive and confirms that all have passed.

**Whole bowel irrigation for intact packets (standard teaching, not in your notes); laparotomy for a ruptured cocaine packet; naloxone infusion for heroin.** In an asymptomatic packer with a normal ECG, polyethylene glycol flushes intact packets through before they break (TOX-09) — even for cocaine; surgery is not needed while the packets hold. Heroin leakage has an antidote, so a naloxone infusion holds the patient while packets pass. Cocaine has none: continuing absorption brings seizures, hyperthermia and arrhythmia that benzodiazepines cannot outrun, so a leaking cocaine packet comes out surgically. Obstruction is the other indication for surgery.
mimic: Body packer vs body stuffer
A packer swallows well-made packets for smuggling (large dose, sealed); a stuffer hastily swallows loosely wrapped drug to evade arrest (smaller dose, leaks early).
traps: “Asymptomatic cocaine packer — surgical removal”
Surgery is for rupture with toxicity or obstruction; intact packets in a well patient get whole bowel irrigation.
“Asymptomatic with a normal ECG — discharge”
Every packet is a potential lethal dose; irrigate and observe until CT shows clearance.
“Endoscopic removal of the packets”
Endoscopy risks tearing a packet; it is generally avoided.
decode: Airport smuggler, no symptoms, radio-opaque packets, normal ECG — management [DocT]
Whole bowel irrigation.
Swallowed cocaine packets, then sudden hypotension, VT and confusion [DocT GT]
Acute packet rupture — benzodiazepines and laparotomy.
REC-04.punch: A body packer is safe only while every packet holds: flush the intact ones through, cover a heroin leak with naloxone, and take a leaking cocaine packet out surgically because nothing else can stop the absorption.

REC-05.intro: Cocaine does two things at once. It blocks reuptake of noradrenaline, dopamine and serotonin, so the patient becomes hot, hypertensive and agitated; and it blocks cardiac sodium channels, as a local anaesthetic does. Most of its harm comes from intense vasoconstriction and that sympathetic storm — which is why calming the brain comes before treating the blood pressure.
why: **Tropane alkaloid; CNS stimulant.** Cocaine is an ester local anaesthetic as well as a stimulant, and that sodium-channel block explains its wide-QRS arrhythmias.

**Hyperthermia, seizures, myocardial infarction, aortic dissection, stroke, rhabdomyolysis and AKI.** Coronary vasospasm, platelet aggregation and higher oxygen demand cause infarction even with normal arteries. Sudden pressure surges tear the aorta and rupture cerebral vessels — intracranial haemorrhage is the complication to fear, not bradycardia, respiratory depression or hypothermia. Agitation and muscle activity break down muscle; heroin causes rhabdomyolysis too, by a different route (immobility and compression after a long down-time), whereas synthetic cannabinoids injure the kidney mostly directly and are the least likely of these to cause it. Smoked or snorted cocaine can also cause diffuse alveolar haemorrhage within 48 hours.

**Benzodiazepines; cooling; aggressive fluids for rhabdomyolysis.** Benzodiazepines reduce central sympathetic outflow, so heart rate, blood pressure, agitation and heat production fall together — they treat the cause. Cooling is active because the set point is normal (TOX-12). Fluids keep urine flowing to clear myoglobin.

**Avoid pure beta-blockers: unopposed alpha stimulation. Use nitrates, calcium-channel blockers or phentolamine.** Cocaine stimulates α- and β-receptors; β₂ vasodilation partly offsets α vasoconstriction. Block β alone (metoprolol, propranolol) and the α effect is left unopposed, worsening coronary spasm and pressure. Nitroglycerin, nitroprusside and calcium-channel blockers (diltiazem, verapamil, nicardipine) dilate vessels without that problem, and phentolamine blocks α directly; aspirin is given as in any ACS.

**Sodium bicarbonate; lidocaine; lipid emulsion.** The wide QRS is sodium-channel block, so bicarbonate overcomes it as in a tricyclic overdose (TOX-07). Lidocaine (class Ib) leaves the channel quickly and is the acceptable anti-arrhythmic if bicarbonate fails; lipid emulsion is a last resort in refractory arrest.
mimic: Cocaine vs amphetamine
Same sympathomimetic picture and same blood-pressure rules; cocaine is short-acting and also widens the QRS, amphetamine lasts many hours (REC-06).
Diffuse alveolar haemorrhage vs pneumothorax after cocaine
Haemoptysis, hypoxaemia and diffuse bilateral infiltrates = alveolar haemorrhage (‘crack lung’); deep inhalation with Valsalva can cause pneumothorax, but that gives no diffuse infiltrates.
traps: “Metoprolol for cocaine chest pain with hypertension and tachycardia”
Contraindicated — unopposed α. Diltiazem, aspirin and lorazepam are all appropriate (REC-14c).
“Labetalol is safe in cocaine toxicity because it also blocks α”

Given IV it is mainly a β-blocker (α:β about 1:7). AHA guidance (2008 statement, 2012 update) calls it ‘may be reasonable’ in hypertensive cocaine ACS only after a vasodilator, and the 2014 guideline advises against β-blockers during acute intoxication; against lorazepam, phentolamine and nitroglycerin it is the exam’s ‘least appropriate’ answer.
“Heroin does not cause rhabdomyolysis”
It does, through immobilisation and compression; among cocaine, methamphetamine, heroin and synthetic cannabinoids, the last is least likely.
decode: Cocaine chest pain with ST elevation (or hypertension and tachycardia) — contraindicated drug [DocT]
Beta-blocker (metoprolol).
Cocaine, BP 223/150, diaphoretic, ST depression — least appropriate: lorazepam, phentolamine, nitroglycerin, labetalol [DocT GT]
Labetalol.
Haemoptysis and diffuse bilateral infiltrates after snorting cocaine [DocT]
Diffuse alveolar haemorrhage.
Complication of cocaine abuse to worry about most [NEET 2025]
Intracranial haemorrhage.
REC-05.punch: Cocaine is a catecholamine storm plus a sodium-channel blocker: calm the brain with benzodiazepines, open the vessels without blocking β alone, and treat the wide QRS with bicarbonate.

parts.q: Cocaine STEMI: reperfusion strategy?
parts.a: **Primary PCI** when available (spasm, dissection and thrombus are common), plus benzodiazepines, nitrates and aspirin; fibrinolysis is second-line because of dissection and haemorrhage risk.

parts.q: Depression, hypersomnia and craving after stopping a stimulant?
parts.a: **Cocaine withdrawal** — a ‘crash’, not an autonomic storm.

REC-06.intro: Amphetamines are indirect sympathomimetics: they push monoamines out of nerve terminals rather than stimulating receptors themselves, so their effect is longer and stronger than cocaine’s. MDMA is the amphetamine with the biggest serotonin effect. At a hot, crowded rave that surge drives temperature up and, through ADH release and heavy drinking, sodium down — and hyperthermia is what kills.
why: **Ecstasy (tablet), Molly (crystal).** Molly is sold as the ‘pure’ powder, though street samples are often adulterated.

**Releases and blocks reuptake of dopamine and serotonin; 5-HT2A agonist.** MDMA enters the terminal through the transporter and reverses it, so serotonin, dopamine and noradrenaline pour into the synapse — increased synaptic release, not direct α- or dopamine-receptor agonism. The serotonin release is far greater than with other amphetamines, which explains the empathy users seek, the jaw clenching and bruxism, and the serotonergic toxicity.

**Serotonin syndrome; also hyperthermia and hyponatraemia (standard teaching, not in your notes).** Excess serotonin gives clonus, hyperreflexia and heat (REC-11, REC-13). The heat is produced, not set: serotonergic and dopaminergic drive, agitation and muscle activity, plus mitochondrial uncoupling in muscle, while vasoconstriction and a hot room stop its loss — the set point is normal and the patient sweats. It drives rhabdomyolysis, DIC and multi-organ failure. Serotonin also releases ADH, and users drink large volumes of water, so a euvolaemic SIADH-type hyponatraemia (urine osmolality >100, urine sodium >30) develops, with cerebral oedema and seizures — especially in young women.

**Parenteral benzodiazepines; nitroglycerine or nicardipine; no beta-blockers; external cooling.** Benzodiazepines lower central drive and so the heat, heart rate and pressure together. If hypertension persists a vasodilator or phentolamine is added; a beta-blocker (propranolol, even labetalol) is avoided for the unopposed-α reason (REC-05). Cooling comes first when the temperature is high, because peak temperature predicts death. Hyponatraemia is treated by severity: mild symptoms, fluid restriction; seizures or coma, 3% saline in 100–150 mL boluses.
mimic: MDMA vs cocaine or methamphetamine
Bruxism and jaw clenching, hyponatraemia and long duration point to MDMA; LSD gives hallucinations with little sympathetic storm.
traps: “Methamphetamine with severe hypertension — labetalol or propranolol”

Beta-blockade leaves α unopposed. DocT keys phentolamine as the first antihypertensive; nicardipine is equally defensible (both listed as alternatives), and benzodiazepines — the true first step — are not offered. The key is disputed.
“Seizures, rhabdomyolysis or intracranial haemorrhage is the most immediate threat after ‘molly’”
Hyperthermia is the killer; the others are downstream of it or rarer. Cool first.
“MDMA hyperthermia is a reset hypothalamic set point or impaired sweating”
It is heat production (muscle activity, mitochondrial uncoupling) with poor heat loss; users sweat and the set point is normal.
“Any MDMA hyponatraemia needs hypertonic saline”
Sodium 128 with only dizziness and a normal neurological examination: fluid restriction. 3% saline is for seizures or coma; demeclocycline is too slow.
“Amphetamines stimulate α-receptors directly”
They are indirect: transporter reversal increases synaptic dopamine and noradrenaline release.
decode: Rave, agitation, hyperthermia, mydriasis, sweating, bruxism [DocT]
MDMA.
‘Molly’ at a festival — most immediate life-threatening complication [DocT]
Hyperthermia leading to multi-organ failure.
Ecstasy, sodium 128, euvolaemic, urine Na 105, only dizzy [DocT GT]
SIADH-type — fluid restriction.
Methamphetamine with severe hypertension and seizures — best antihypertensive [DocT; DocT GT]
Phentolamine (keyed; nicardipine also defensible) — never a beta-blocker.
REC-06.punch: MDMA is the serotonin amphetamine: the serotonin surge brings heat, clonus and ADH release, so temperature and sodium decide survival — cool first, sedate with benzodiazepines, and never use a beta-blocker.

REC-07.intro: Every feature of the sympathomimetic toxidrome is the fight-or-flight response turned up and left on. Cocaine, amphetamines, MDMA and cathinones flood the synapses with noradrenaline and dopamine, so each organ shows its sympathetic action — and the opposite drug class, an opioid, is the one that cannot produce it.
why: **CNS: euphoria, agitation, psychosis, seizures.** Dopamine excess gives euphoria, then paranoia and psychosis; at high levels the cortex seizes, and agitation adds heat and acidosis.
**Neuromuscular: hyperreflexia, tremor.** Central drive and β₂ stimulation of muscle make reflexes brisk and produce tremor — but without the inducible clonus that marks serotonin toxicity (REC-12).

**Autonomic: hyperthermia, sweating, mydriasis.** Heat comes from muscle activity and vasoconstriction that stops skin heat loss. Sweating continues because sympathetic sweat fibres use acetylcholine and are driven, not blocked — the key difference from the anticholinergic patient (TOX-03). The pupils dilate through α₁ action.
**Cardiovascular: tachycardia, hypertension, arrhythmia.** β₁ stimulation speeds the heart and α₁ vasoconstriction raises the pressure, raising oxygen demand while narrowing coronary supply.
**GI: nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea.** Non-specific, but bowel sounds are present, unlike the silent bowel of anticholinergic poisoning.
mimic: Sympathomimetic vs anticholinergic
Both hot, fast and dilated; the sympathomimetic patient sweats and has bowel sounds, the anticholinergic is dry with retention.
Sympathomimetic vs serotonin syndrome
Both sweat with brisk reflexes; clonus belongs to serotonin toxicity.
traps: “Agitation, tachycardia, mydriasis and diaphoresis — anticholinergic”
Diaphoresis excludes it: anticholinergic skin is dry. This is sympathomimetic, and cocaine or amphetamine causes it; the least likely agent is an opioid (miosis, sedation, bradycardia).
“Hyperreflexia means serotonin syndrome”
Sympathomimetics give brisk reflexes too; clonus is the serotonin sign.
decode: Agitation, tachycardia, dilated pupils, diaphoresis — toxidrome, and the agent least likely to cause it [DocT]
Sympathomimetic; opioid.
Same stem, option ‘anticholinergic; cocaine’ [DocT]
Wrong twice — sweating excludes anticholinergic, and cocaine does cause this picture.
REC-07.punch: The sympathomimetic toxidrome is adrenaline on every organ — hot, fast, hypertensive and dilated — and, unlike the anticholinergic, still sweating with bowel sounds present.

REC-08.intro: Classic hallucinogens are 5-HT2A agonists in the cortex: they scramble sensory filtering and give visions and synaesthesia. A second group — phencyclidine, ketamine and dextromethorphan — block the NMDA receptor and dissociate mind from body. None has an antidote; the danger is behaviour, panic and occasionally heat, and agitation is treated with benzodiazepines.
why: **LSD: ergot-derived; synaesthesia, panic, hyperthermia.** Made from lysergic acid of the ergot fungus and active in micrograms; strong 5-HT2A agonism mixes the senses and can cause ‘bad trips’, with mild sympathetic stimulation and heat at large doses.
**Psilocybin: magic mushrooms; active form psilocin.** Psilocybin is a prodrug, dephosphorylated to psilocin, which acts at 5-HT2A.
**Mescaline: phenylethylamine (peyote).** It shares the amphetamine backbone, which is why it carries some sympathetic effects with its visions.

**Phencyclidine: angel dust; nystagmus, violence.** NMDA block gives dissociation with analgesia, so patients become violent and injure themselves without noticing. Horizontal, vertical or rotatory nystagmus is its bedside signature (TOX-05).
**Ketamine: NMDA antagonist; dissociation.** The shorter-acting relative of PCP: dissociation, nystagmus, raised heart rate and pressure, with airway reflexes and breathing usually preserved.
**Salvia: salvinorin A.** A κ-opioid agonist rather than a serotonin or NMDA drug; intense, very brief dissociation.
mimic: Classic hallucinogen vs dissociative
LSD and psilocybin (5-HT2A) alter perception; PCP, ketamine and dextromethorphan (NMDA) dissociate and add nystagmus.
PCP vs sympathomimetic
Both agitated, hypertensive and violent; nystagmus points to PCP.
traps: “Ketamine is a GABA agonist”
It is an NMDA antagonist (REC-14d).
“Psilocybin is the active molecule”
It is a prodrug; psilocin acts.
“Haloperidol to sedate dextromethorphan or PCP agitation”
Benzodiazepines (lorazepam) are the chemical sedation of choice; dextromethorphan is often co-formulated with paracetamol, so check a paracetamol level.
decode: Dextromethorphan agitation — chemical sedation [Marrow]
Lorazepam.
Violent, analgesic, vertical nystagmus [pattern]
Phencyclidine.
REC-08.punch: Hallucinogens split into 5-HT2A agonists that distort perception (LSD, psilocybin, mescaline) and NMDA antagonists that dissociate with nystagmus (PCP, ketamine) — neither has an antidote, so quiet and benzodiazepines are the treatment.

REC-09.sub: Toxicology → Hallucinogens & Sedatives → Sedative street drugs
REC-09.intro: Flunitrazepam and GHB are both used to sedate a victim without their knowledge because they are tasteless in a drink, act fast and erase memory. Both enhance GABA inhibition, so the picture is sedation and amnesia with vital signs that stay surprisingly normal until coma is deep.
why: **Rohypnol: a benzodiazepine 10 times as potent as diazepam; acts in 10–20 minutes for 4–6 hours; detected as a benzodiazepine on screening.** A 1–2 mg dose sedates strongly, with anterograde amnesia; in practice sedation and amnesia often last 8–12 hours or more, and the low dose means routine immunoassays often miss it. Alcohol deepens the sedation and respiratory depression.

**Gamma-hydroxybutyrate: liquid, mixed with alcohol; euphoria, amnesia, hypotonia, then sudden coma; supportive care.** GHB acts mainly on GABA-B receptors with a steep dose–response curve, so coma follows within minutes — often with bradycardia and myoclonus — and the patient wakes abruptly a few hours later. Airway support is all that is needed.

**CNS depression with near-normal vital signs and reflexes.** Sedative-hypnotics depress the cortex and reticular activating system long before the brainstem centres for breathing and circulation — unless alcohol or an opioid is added (TOX-04).
mimic: Sedative-hypnotic or GHB vs opioid coma
Opioid: pinpoint pupils and a very slow respiratory rate, reversed by naloxone. Sedative: variable pupils, near-normal breathing; GHB coma also ends abruptly.
traps: “Flumazenil to reverse a suspected Rohypnol drink”
Rarely given — seizure risk in dependence or mixed ingestion; support the airway (TOX-01).
“A negative screen excludes a spiked drink”
GHB is not on the standard immunoassay, and flunitrazepam is often missed.
decode: Sudden coma at a party, wakes abruptly after 3 hours [pattern]
GHB.
Deep coma with near-normal vital signs [pattern]
Sedative-hypnotic toxidrome.
REC-09.punch: Flunitrazepam and GHB both deepen GABA inhibition — sedation and amnesia with near-normal vital signs — and GHB adds a sudden coma that ends as suddenly, needing only airway support.
fix: Flunitrazepam is detected as a benzodiazepine; lasts 4–6 hours
Routine urine benzodiazepine screens often miss it (specific assays needed), and sedation and amnesia often last 8–12 hours or more.

REC-10.intro: Volatile solvents — toluene, butane, propane — are inhaled from a bag or rag. They behave like inhaled anaesthetics: fat-soluble, taken up and cleared through the lungs within minutes, so even deep coma lifts quickly once the vapour is gone. The acute danger is the heart; the chronic danger is to lipid-rich tissue, especially the brain.
why: **Glue, lighter refills, spray deodorants; street children.** Cheap, legal and everywhere, so they are the drug of the poorest and youngest users (REC-01).

**Sudden sniffing death syndrome: arrhythmia (myocardium sensitised to catecholamines).** Solvents make the myocardium excitable, so an adrenaline surge — fright, being chased, sudden exertion — triggers VF; rebreathing hypoxia adds to it. Approach calmly, and use adrenaline with great care.

**Neurological, lung, liver and kidney damage.** Solvents dissolve into myelin: chronic toluene gives leukoencephalopathy, ataxia and dementia, and also distal renal tubular acidosis with severe hypokalaemia (normal anion gap). n-Hexane causes peripheral neuropathy; chlorinated solvents injure the liver.
traps: “GCS 3 recovering to 15 within 10 minutes — smoked heroin”
Heroin coma lasts hours unless naloxone is given; cannabis does not cause coma; only a solvent clears through the lungs that fast.
“Sudden death in huffing is from asphyxia alone”
The main mechanism is catecholamine-sensitised VF, often triggered by fright or exertion.
decode: 16-year-old, GCS 3, sitting up talking with GCS 15 ten minutes later [DocT]
Inhaled solvent (glue).
Teenager collapses while running from police after sniffing glue [pattern]
Sudden sniffing death — VF.
REC-10.punch: Solvents are cheap anaesthetic vapours: they wear off in minutes, but they sensitise the heart to adrenaline — so fright can cause fatal VF — and with chronic use they dissolve the brain’s myelin.

REC-11.sub: Toxicology → Hyperthermic Toxidromes → Serotonin syndrome vs NMS
REC-11.intro: Both syndromes give a hot, confused, rigid patient on psychiatric drugs. But they arise from opposite neurochemistry: serotonin syndrome is too much serotonin, NMS too little dopamine action. Too much serotonin excites — fast onset, clonus, brisk reflexes; too little dopamine freezes — slow onset, rigidity, slow reflexes. The drug history usually gives it away.
why: **Cause: serotonin syndrome — excess serotonin, usually two serotonergic drugs; NMS — dopamine blockade, or stopping a dopamine agonist.** Serotonin syndrome follows adding a second serotonergic drug — an antidepressant plus tramadol, linezolid or a cough remedy (dextromethorphan) for a cold (TOX-05). NMS follows a D₂ antagonist — typical or atypical antipsychotics (haloperidol, olanzapine), metoclopramide — or abrupt withdrawal of levodopa, as in a Parkinson’s patient who stops getting it after admission. A psychiatric card with procyclidine (given for antipsychotic side-effects) implies an antipsychotic. Dopamine agonists themselves do not cause it.

**Onset: serotonin syndrome under 12 hours; NMS 1–3 days.** Serotonin excess is direct, so it appears within hours of the change; NMS builds as dopamine block accumulates — days to a few weeks after starting or raising the drug.
**Pupils: serotonin syndrome dilated; NMS normal.** Serotonin excess drives the sympathetic system; dopamine block does not.

**Tone: serotonin syndrome increased, in the legs; NMS lead-pipe rigidity.** Spinal serotonin excitation raises tone mostly in the legs; loss of basal-ganglia dopamine gives generalised, uniform lead-pipe rigidity.

**Reflexes: serotonin syndrome hyperreflexia and clonus; NMS bradyreflexia.** The most reliable discriminator: clonus or myoclonus means serotonin; ‘no clonus’ in a rigid febrile patient points to NMS.
**Bowel: serotonin syndrome hyperactive; NMS normal.** Gut serotonin drives motility, so serotonin excess gives diarrhoea.

**Treatment: serotonin syndrome — cyproheptadine; NMS — bromocriptine, dantrolene.** Both start with stopping the drug, benzodiazepines and cooling. Cyproheptadine blocks 5-HT2A (REC-13). Bromocriptine replaces the missing dopamine action and is the conventional drug of choice; dantrolene relaxes muscle by blocking calcium release and is the adjunct. Neither has trial evidence, and dantrolene has none at all in stimulant hyperthermia.
mimic: NMS vs malignant hyperthermia
Both rigid and hot with high CK; MH happens in theatre after a volatile agent or suxamethonium, with rising ETCO₂.
Serotonin syndrome vs opioid withdrawal or anticholinergic
All can be tachycardic with dilated pupils. Withdrawal gives yawning, lacrimation and piloerection without fever or clonus; the anticholinergic patient is dry with a silent bowel.
traps: “NMS drug of choice — dantrolene”
DocT keys bromocriptine; dantrolene is the adjunct. A Marrow item keys dantrolene for antipsychotic-related rigidity and catatonia — if both are offered, bromocriptine is the conventional answer.
“A trial (HAT, RAMP, DAHS) supports dantrolene in amphetamine hyperthermia”
No trial does — those names are invented; stimulant heat is central drive and muscle activity, not a ryanodine-receptor leak.
“Rigid and febrile 2 weeks after starting olanzapine and clomipramine — the antidepressant”
No clonus, rigidity, raised CK and transaminases mean NMS from the high-dose antipsychotic; atypicals cause it too. Lithium alone causes it only rarely (case reports) and is not the answer.
“Fever, tremor, myoclonus and sweating on antidepressants — NMS or anticholinergic”
Myoclonus and sweating mean serotonin syndrome; a cold remedy was the second drug (REC-14e).

Bromocriptine.
Antipsychotic started 2 weeks ago, rigid, no clonus, diaphoretic, BP 185/90 [DocT GT]
